subtopic: ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES IN CONNECTION WITH PARCEL DELIVERIES OVERSEAS
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question of the Postmaster General. I note that the Toronto board of control is asking the Postmaster General to investigate charges that Canadians overseas have not been receiving parcels from home, and have received parcels which have been opened prior to arrival at their destination. According to the press dispatch one of the members of the board of
control stated that thefts had increased until it was now estimated that only sixty per cent of the cigarettes sent to Canadian soldiers have been reaching them. If these statements be true, it would appear to indicate that a serious situation exists. I should like the Postmaster General, if he is now in a position to do so, to comment on the statements and indicate what steps his department is taking to ensure safe delivery, subject to the usual ocean risks, of all mail and parcels addressed to our armed forces in other parts of the world.

subtopic: ALLEGED IRREGULARITIES IN CONNECTION WITH PARCEL DELIVERIES OVERSEAS
speechtext: I saw the press report and heard the radio news, but as yet no resolution has been received by the department or by myself. I wired the board of control at Toronto, and also controller Fred Hamilton, who made certain charges, asking for particulars, and asking that they forward the information to me. Of course I shall make a full statement, but in the meantime I would say that the reports received from officials in the postal corps overseas, and from officials in Canada, do not bear out the statements appearing in the press report.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
maintopic: LEAVE TO SOLDIERS FOR WORK ON FARMS
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) inquired with regard to the terms upon which agricultural leave is being granted by the department. The' terms of this leave are set out in a circular letter which was sent to the general officers commanding both the Atlantic and Pacific commands, the commanders of Borden and Peta-wawa camps, the general officers commanding the sixth, seventh and eighth divisions and the district officers commanding. I suggest that perhaps the best thing to do would be to table the circular letter and ask, with the leave of the house, that it be printed in Votes and Proceedings.
May I just say that I do not want the hopes of the members of the house, or those who are engaged in farming, to be raised too high on account of this circular. The matter has been very carefully considered and the department is doing the best it can to conform with the desires and the wishes of agriculturists across Canada and to help in any way they can in that respect. But the department has certain responsibilities and those responsibilities have to be safeguarded.
Since the circular letter will be printed in Votes and Proceedings, I will not attempt to summarize it completely, but subject to the conditions in the circular I may say that those who are eligible to apply for spring seeding
Canadian Forces

leave are those who have some experience in farm work and who in the opinion of the general, divisional or district officer commanding can be spared with due regard to the military exigencies existing at the time. The circular applies, first, to those who are on the personnel of the home war establishment of district depots. That means administrative and training staffs of the district depots. Second, personnel on strength of district depots who are not awaiting dispatch to basic training centres or who, having completed training, are not awaiting allocation as reinforcements or to units. Third, veterans guard who can be spared from their duties, and, fourth, not more than 5 per cent of personnel employed on operational units, provided such personnel have completed their individual training and are not earmarked for overseas service. The majority of the troops both on the east and west coast are in the operational units.
The method to be adopted is to have the soldier make application to his commanding officer, who, if he recommends, will forward the same to his next superior officer, whoever it may be, for official approval. In this regard there has been some complaint as to the slowness of the operation. This has been the complaint in connection with applications for leave in previous instances, not so much with regard to agricultural leave as with regard to applications for compassionate leave.
In connection with this leave, instructions are going out impressing on all concerned that the applications should be dealt with promptly. We realize that he gives twice who gives quickly. I do want to impress upon the house and the country that it is most desirable that the applicant assist by submitting to the commanding officer the necessary information on two points. First, his qualifications and his experience, and the likelihood of his being really efficient and effective in connection with farming operations, having regard to his past experience. Second, the necessity for his services in the particular place where he desires to go. '
_ I assure the hon. member that with that information at hand, every endeavour will be made to deal with the applications as quickly and as sympathetically as possible.

I remember back in 1927 and 1928 or thereabouts when our navy consisted of the Rainbow and the Niobe, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) spoke in this house and referred to our navy as consisting of these two ships and he asked: Where is our fleet now? And he answered in derision: Tied up in a garage at Halifax. Ah, but he does not say that now. Our fleet is to-day doing a man-sized job, sailing and patrolling the seven seas, and we are all proud of it. It is doing forty per cent of the convoy work in the north Atlantic. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to have permission, if I may, to answer the question. I think that it is important that the facts be made known, as there is some present unrest in the plant mentioned.
Some weeks ago, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I told the house that no decision had been made with regard to the continuation of the tank order at the Angus shops. Since then the changing strategy of war has made it evident that we should not undertake further tank production in that shop after the present order is completed. Orders have been placed for the full capacity of the shop in connection with the escort shipbuilding programme, and my first intimation from the management was that all the present employees would be required. Accordingly, I so advised my colleague the Minister of Labour, and he so advised a delegation of employees from the Angus shops. But within the last two days I have been advised by the management that there will be a lay-off at the Angus shops of approximately 1,100 men, about 485 men between April 1 and April 15, and about 620 between April 15 and April 30. I may say that my colleague is arranging through national selective service to transfer these men to other employment where they are urgently required. I think that the men to be transferred will not be worse off after the transfer than they are to-day.

Mr. Speaker, in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) on Monday, March 22, I intimated that the question of Canadians going into the northern part of Maine to harvest maple sugar was under consideration.
Along the international boundary between the province of Quebec and the state of Maine there has been an annual migration of families to United States territory for the purpose of harvesting the maple sugar crop. My information is that the sap is collected in northern Maine and brought into Canada 72537-98}
in bond and the finished product is shipped back to the United States and sold. This movement has taken place over a very long period of time. At the suggestion of the government of the province of Quebec and the United States authorities and because of the desirability of assuring the harvesting of this crop, arrangements have been made to permit a limited number again this year to work in the Maine sugar camps. Approximately one hundred and twenty-five families, consisting of men, women and children, are being allowed to cross the border on the understanding that Quebec farm work will not suffer and that the absence will not exceed twenty-nine days.
The mobilization boards will, of course, be consulted with respect to any men who are in the designated military age classes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, part of the subamendment moved by the leader of this group expresses regret at-
-the failure of the government to provide for increases in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, or to make adequate provisions for veterans of the last or the present war, or their widows and dependents.
Judging by the large number of faon. members sitting in all parts of this house who have complained about the inadequate provision for the old age pensioners, it might have been expected that something would be done to make their lot somewhat easier. I find in the estimates tabled by the minister :a short time ago that the amount which the : government proposes to spend this year to assist the aged and the blind totals $31,246,500. According to the 1942 year book, there were 186,834 old age pensioners and 6,208 blind pensioners in Canada, a total of 193,042. This means that the Dominion of Canada is spending about $163 a year, or a little less than $14 a month, to assist each of those who are over seventy and have been unable to provide for themselves in the evening of life. I find that in the same estimates we provide pensions for retired judges. There are only fifty-five, but they receive according to statute $273,133.31, or $4,966 each, that is, over $413 per month. It is difficult to justify such bigh pensions for one group of our old people who have received a generous allowance during a lifetime, when the average pension received by the old age pensioner is less than $20 per month.
I have here a resolution, passed by the Eston branch of the Canadian Legion, which- -records its protest against the inadequacy of the maintenance and unemployment benefits of $9 per week for single men, and $13 per week for married men, as set forth in acts and orders in council governing the rehabilitation of returned soldiers: that we condemn the limitations contained in those acts and orders in council, and deplore the fact that reestablishment measures, so far, have been based upon the presumption of the existence of a set of post-war [DOT]conditions which we feel should not be taken into consideration in the framing of an effective rehabilitation programme.
In the brief which the Eston branch submit, they point out that-
In New Zealand, the old age pension allowance is thirty shillings per week per individual, which is approximately $60 per month per married couple-eight dollars per month more than we allow a married returned soldier.
(Mr. Lockhart.]
They mention a press dispatch from Saskatoon stating that the collegiate board agreed that $85 per month was inadequate for janitors, and increased their salaries to $102.50 and $105 per month. I may mention that the Eston branch has an enviable record in connection with every possible project to further the war effort. More consideration should have been given by the government to providing for the needs of those who have risked their lives in the present conflict.
There have been two or three speeches during the present debate which in my opinion might very well not have been made; I refer to addresses of the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly), the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward), and the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). It would appear that these hon. members hate the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation so bitterly that they find difficulty in thinking straight when they get wound up.

speechtext:
eration hold; and thus you confuse them. I suggest that we should describe fascism as it is and accept the point of view that members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this house and in the country are anxious to do everything they can to see that fascism is destroyed.
While our views differ from the views expressed by the former leader of the opposition, we do make our contribution. He would like to see the soldiers come back to the good old *days. Well, the party he supports was in office from 1930 to 1935, and while I have no special brief for the present administration, I ask hon. members to think back to those years and consider whether they should like to have an administration that would do as little about unemployment and depressed conditions as did the government under Viscount Bennett. If there ever was a man in Canada who had something at stake it was the man who was prime minister of Canada from 1930 to 1935. He had made a success under the present system, he had tremendous energy, and if capitalism could be made to work surely he would have made it work. The hon. member for York-Sunbury was a member of that government.
I am sorry time does not permit me to deal with three cases I have here, men who fought in the last war, who are now doing useful work in Canada, but for- whom during the Bennett regime the best the Conservative government in Canada and Saskatchewan could do was to set aside $100 from each of the federal and provincial governments for a whole year to reestablish them. They were given $50 to build a house and $100 to buy *equipment; they received $10 a month for food and within a period of a year they were expected to become self-supporting.
I have one case here, that of Mr. Sig Watland-I have mentioned it in the house before-a man whose standard of living was forced down to $10 a month during those terrible years. I have told the house of the trouble I had in getting him off his homestead and down here. Here is what he wrote to me last week:
I had no difficulty in obtaining a position as senior draftsman with the John T. Hepburn Company with a salary of $210 a month. During the last two months I have been doing catalogue drawing. This is specialized work and very few draftsmen can do it, as any draftsman can tell you. I am well pleased here. I am.geting my farm paid for. My family have had cash in the house this winter and consequently have been off relief. My eldest daughter enlisted in the CWAC last summer, and has been stationed in Ottawa this winter. Together with my. income tax and the $10 per month I am paying on victory bonds I am just paying Margaret's allowance in the army and this is a great . satisfaction to me.

It is a great satisfaction to any Canadian to see a man who during those years in which the hon. member for York-Sunbury was occupying a cabinet position was not considered worth any more to society than $10 a month, a trained mechanical draftsman who now after all he has been through is demonstrating that he can come back and earn $210 a month.
I would not accuse the hon. member for York-Sunbury of plagiarism, but I read an article by David Low which appeared in the Toronto Star the other day, about Colonel Blimp, and there is a remarkable similarity between the views expressed by Colonel Blimp and those of the hon. members for York-Sunbury, Wood Mountain and Dauphin. The article represents Colonel Blimp as saying:
Now we have these dashed planners running about, planning everything. Absolute anarchy. Fellows wanting to improve the British way of life. Dashed unpatriotic. These planners say they're out to avoid chaos. Say what you like about chaos. It provides freedom for enterprise and initiative. And what's going to be needed more after the war than enterprise and initiative?
Then there's the bishops. Public control of credit, land and water! Dash it, you can't mix religion with business. It's unethical. What this country needs is a religious revival against the teachings of the Archbishop of Canterbury. And now this fellow Beveridge comes along, wanting to undermine the stability of the country with security. Everybody knows that insurance discourages thrift even more than saving.
Then he has something to say about postwar conditions:
True, post-war conditions may involve some reorganization for efficiency. But the best people to handle all that are the big industrialists. It stands to reason that private people know more about what is good for the country than the M.P's, because private people are inspired by the profit motive, which is the spirit of service.
A lot of bosh is talked by the dashed Reds about the profit motive, but you have got to have people making profits or you cannot have business development (except in Russia, where they don't understand economics). The great danger of concentrating industrial power under public control is that any adventurer may get the majority of votes, then command the lot. Too dangerous. Much safer to hand over the whole thing to private monopolies that are not dependent on votes and cannot be interfered with.
Colonel Blimp made a "powerful" speech last week-I forget whether it was in the House of Commons or the American Congress.
"It appears certain now," he said, "that victory will be won as soon as we have defeated the enemy. But I'll never sheathe the sword until freedom is restored and all those who disagree with me are locked up. Let us put our backs to the wall with stiff upper lips and all pull together against collectivism, and the future will be before us."

The Budget-Mr. McGeer
I do not expect that a majority of the members in this house will support our amendment. But I do hope that the opinions expressed in the debate by the members of this group will receive favourable consideration by the ministry at an early day so that Canadians may make their greatest contribution as partners in a great struggle.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are now discussing the fourth budget of the war. This budget has some marks of great distinction as compared with former budgets in other times of war. If one were called upon to measure in a sentence the difference between the budgets in this time of war and the budgets from 1914-18, that is, the budgets for war under Liberal leadership and the budgets for war under Tory administration, one could find it in the difference in the rates of interest paid and1 in the methods now adopted in regard to finance. To-day we have no five and a half per cent tax-free war bonds; in contrast we have a ministry of finance that is raising an enormous loan at the rate of three-quarters of one per cent. History is in the making in many ways, no less in the sphere of financial administration than otherwise. I remember that during the dark days of the depression, when millions of jobs were crying to be done and millions of people remained in artificial idleness, the governor of the Bank of England brushed aside the clamorous voice of monetary reform with the cryptic declaration: "The dogs bark but the caravan moves on." Well, Mr. Speaker, time and history move on; but it is well to remember that it is in war time that the dealers in debt always reap their greatest harvest. It should never be forgotten that when the dogs of war break the leash to bedevil mankind, the hounds of usury run free. I remember my own puny efforts to help improve the lot of Canadians during the years of the pathetic depression of the Bennett administration.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am no more adept at that than the former leader of the Tory party. To-day, however, I did not want to deal with the controversial issue of monetary reform so much as to draw attention to some of the
things that are taking place in the history which the men and women of our day and generation are making. '
In the toll of time we have witnessed recently the passing of a great American and a great Canadian. In the passing of Mr. J. P. Morgan and Sir Edward Beatty we see something of the passing of the golden age of laissez-faire, the golden age which reared a rugged individualism, which in turn laid the great foundations upon which our modem commerce and industry are founded. It was my privilege to contest with the Canadian Pacific Railway, during the presidency of Sir Edward Beatty, the issue of the mountain differential in British Columbia.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At how much per day?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At a very good fee for very good service rendered. In fact it came to be known as the case in which the faith to move mountains was required. Well, we did not move the mountains, but we did remove the mountain differential on grain and made Vancouver the greatest grain port in the Dominion of Canada. It was my privilege to come to know Sir Edward Beatty during that period of time; and later as mayor of the city of Vancouver I had the privilege of conferring upon him the freedom of that city. I found him to be a great Canadian and a great leader, one who commanded' the respect of all Canadians, who was revered and loved by every member of the great staff that maintained the Canadian Pacific Railway, from the humblest apprentice and office boy to the highest executive. His passing marks the passing of a great era of constructive enterprise in Canada.
As we mourn the loss of Sir Edward Beatty, we are all grateful for the fact that the war leader of the British empire has been restored to health and is again fulfilling the greatest chapter in his amazing career. I think everyone who has read Churchill's magnificent record of the life of the Duke of Marlborough cannot help but realize the profound influence which that remarkable contribution to British empire history has had upon the statecraft and the success of Winston Churchill. In appreciating the life work of the Duke of Marlborough, Churchill has said:
Marlborough's victorious sword established upon sure foundations the constitutional and parliamentary structure of our country almost as it has come down to us to-day. He carried all that was best in the life work of Oliver Cromwell and William III to an abiding conclusion. ... He animated the war at sea no less than on land and established till the present time the British naval supremacy in the Mediterranean. His eye ranged far across the oceans, and the foundations of British dominions
The Budget-Mr. McGeer

were launched or strengthened as the result of his continental policy. He was for six years the commander in chief of the allies, but though subject, the virtual master of England, he was head of the most glorious administration in her history.
Churchill in reality is reliving the life of his illustrious predecessor. He is a master scholar in the most difficult art of history, and I was particularly impressed by his expression in regard to history's interpretation. He says:
All men and events are moving forward together in a throng. Each individual decision is the result of all the forces at work at any given moment; and the passage of even a few years enables, nay compels, men and peoples to think, feel and act quite differently without any insincerity or baseness.
No doubt my friends in the Progressive Conservative party will get a little comfort out of that. He goes on to say:
In understanding history, if readers will look back over the last three or four years of their own lives, or that of their country, and pass in detailed review events as they occurred and successive opinions they have formed upon them they will appreciate the pervading mutability of all human affairs. Combinations long abhorred become the order of the day. Ideas last year deemed inadmissible form the pavement of daily routine. Political antagonists make common cause and abandoning old friends, find new . . . The popularity of governments departs as the too bright hopes on which it was founded fade into normal and general disappointments. But all this seems natural to those who live through a period of change.
Churchill, born a blue-blooded Tory, serving the demands of progress left the Tory party and became the great crusading knight of British Liberalism. In that great era of reform at the beginning of this century, when old-age pensions, anti-sweat laws, the rights of trade union organizations, unemployment insurance and the right of parliament to be free from interference in fiscal matters from the House of Lords, ' wrere burning issues, Churchill became the reincarnation of St. George, and the House of Lords was the dragon of reactionism sustaining the unrighteousness of privileged monopoly.
In those days I was serving my time as an iron moulder and vitally interested in the labour leadership and the influence of great men like Samuel Gompers of the American Federation of Labor. But we young men of Canada looked to Churchill as much as to our labour leader for the reforms that we hoped would come. We looked forward to the reading of his speeches with hopeful confidence. Let me quote from one of them, typical of his attack upon the Tory government of England in that day:
_ We want a government that will think a little more about the toilers at the bottom of

the mines, and a little less about the fluctuations of the share market in London. We want a government which instead of looking mainly abroad will look mainly if not, I think, entirely at home. We want a government and policy which will think the condition of a slum in an English city is not less worthy of the attention of statesmen and of parliament than the jungle of Somaliland. We know very well what to expect from a great leader of a protectionist party

a party of great vested interests: corruption at home, aggression to cover it up abroad, the trickery of tariff juggles, and tyranny of a party machine, sentiment by the bucketful, patriotism by the imperial pint, the open hand at the public exchequer, the open door at the public house, dear food for the millions, cheap labour for the millionaire.
That was the Churchill who laid the foundation for the faith and confidence that the working masses have placed in him. in this hour of England's crisis. It was during that period that his influence was brought to the Dominion of Canada, and it was then that Sir Wilfrid Laui'ier established the first Department of Labour, and called upon a young Canadian to be the first minister to preside over that department, who afterwards became the Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, enjoying the greatest measure of confidence that has ever been extended to any prime minister in the history of our nation's political life. Not only that, but he became- and to some degree through the medium of his own statesmanship-the leader of a united Dominion of Canada which, as Churchill has declared, became in the world's greatest crisis the linchpin between the British empire and the United States of America. Thus in the golden threads of history we find the public service of Churchill, the war leader of the empire, and Mackenzie King, the war leader of Canada, linked together, just as we find the history of our own dominion inseparably blended with that of the empire.
Just as the history of the house of Marlborough and the British empire was the inspiration to Churchill, the history of our young dominion offers to us the inspiration of our Canadian future.
As I look back upon our history and think of what the fathers of confederation laboured to found, I remember with regard and respect some of the expressions they coined in those days not so far away. Back in 1824 William Lyon Mackenzie, writing to Canning, said this:
A union of all the colonies, with a government suitably poised and modelled, so as to have under its eye the resources of our whole territory and having the means in its power to administer impartial justice in all its bounds, to no one part at the expense of another, -would require few boons from Britain, and would advance her interests much more in a few years

The Budget-Mr. McGeer
than the bare rights of possession of a barren, uncultivated wilderness of lake and forest, with some three or four inhabitants to the square mile, can do in centuries.
That hope of "a self-governing dominion empowered to administer impartial justice, in all its bounds," came as a right to Canadians, and it came from the British parliament. And the hope that it would prove a boon to Great Britain has been more than, fulfilled.
Yes, there were other thoughts expressed by the men who laid the foundations for this dominion. They were linked then, as is this great conflict of to-day, with the hope of freedom. George Etienne Cartier, speaking on confederation, declared:
We cannot by law make the differences of race disappear, but I am convinced that the Anglo-Canadians and the FrenchUanachans will appreciate the advantages of their position. Set side by side, like a great family, their contact will produce a happy spirit of emulation. The diversity of races will in spirit, believe me, contribute to the common prosperity. The whole difficulty will be in the manner of rendering justice to minorities. In Upper Canada the Roman Catholics will be in the minority, in Lower Canada it will be the Protestants who will be in the minority, whilst in the maritime provinces the two communions will equalize each other. Is it possible then to suppose that the general government or the provincial govern-merits can become guilty of arbitrary acts. What would be the result, even supposing that one of the provincial governments should attempt it? Measures of such a character would undoubtedly be repudiated by the mass of the people. There is no reason then to fear that it will ever be sought to deprive a minority of ' its rights.
Sir John A. Macdonald was inspired no less by the same hope of security for minorities, which he expressed in these words:
So long, too, as we form a portion of the British empire, we shall have the example of her free institutions, of the high standard of the character of her statesmen and public men, of the purity of her legislation, and the upright administration of her laws.
We shall enjoy here that which is the great test of constitutional freedom-we shall have the rights of the minority respected. In all countries the rights of the majority take care of themselves, but it is only in countries like England, enjoying constitutional liberty, and safe from the tyranny of a single despot or of an unbridled democracy, that the rights of the minorities are regarded."
But it remained for a great Canadian, a man who had the universal love and respect of all the dominion, a French Canadian, a Roman Catholic, a man who was prime minister of this dominion from 1896 to 1911, to declare the extent to which freedom in Canada has been sustained when he said:
England has proved at all times that she can fight her own battles, but if the day were ever to come when England was in danger, let the bugle sound, let the fires be lit on the hills, and
in all parts of the colonies, though we might not be able to do much, whatever we can do shall be done by the colonies to help her.
The sun in his daily career does not shed its light upon any people on the face of the earth enjoying more liberty than my countrymen of French extraction. And my last words to the doubters, to the scoffers, is that freedom is worth fighting for and worth dying for.
We have not forgotten the dark days of 1940 when France was overwhelmed and England beleaguered stood behind the barricades of her ancient island home. It was then that Churchill came forward to declare and to demonstrate that England in danger is always England at her best. He said:
We shall fight on to the end. ... We shall never surrender. And even if, which I do not for a moment believe, this island or a large part of it were subjugated and starving, then our empire beyond the seas, armed and guarded by the British fleet, will carry on its struggle until in God's good time the new world with all its power and might sets forth to the liberation and rescue of the old.
His faith has been vindicated. To-day upon this continent we are realizing the fruits of a great experiment. We have seen the reconciliation of two great races, each retaining its religion, laws, customs and institutions, living together and building together in one great national home. But the experiment went further than that. It carried on the doctrines of the Rush-Bagot treaty of 1818, under which the great lakes were disarmed and all the boundaries between the United States and the British colonies were freed from fortifications. Canada, with her French and English, as a sovereign nation is working out the fulfilment of a partnership with the United States which has brought about the development of the continent of North America to a point where to-day it is the hope of freedom throughout all the world. Yes, that great work has fulfilled the fondest hopes of the fathers of confederation, and it offers to the whole world something of the kind of relations under which all men in all places and at all times can live and dwell together in peace.
In this war, testing whether or not governments established on the principle of human freedom can be maintained against the effort to establish world domination upon the exclusive foundation of human bondage, Canada is playing a part which should lift Canadians above the petty bickerings and conflicts of party politics and up to the level of service and sacrifice which is being displayed upon every battle front. There is no front to-day on which Canadians are not to be found and on which the product of Canadian war indust ry is not making its contribution.
The Budget-Mr. McGeer

In times of crisis, of course, new declarations appear. To-day we have the Atlantic charter with its new ideals expressed in the terms of the four great freedoms-freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom from fear, and freedom from want. I think we should add another one, freedom from the slavery of involuntary debt.
For a brief moment I should like to touch upon the history of Canada in the realm of constructive finance. I have studied the life of Abraham Lincoln. I feel that in his executive administration of the United States he founded some new concepts of political economy. When Lincoln came to the presidency of the United States that nation was carrying the debt load of the Mexican war. Many there were at that time who declared that because of financial weakness and incapacity the federal government lacked the strength to subdue a revolution of the proportions which brought on the civil war. But Lincoln had been a student of finance. He had married into the banking circles of Kentucky when he married Mary Todd. He was a representative of the bankers for six years on the floor of the legislature of the state of Illinois and he came to the White House equipped' with a knowledge and understanding of the techniques of private bankers and finance, greatly superior to that of many members of this house to-day.
He tried some seven different forms of currency-at that time there were seven thousand banks in the United States-and finally he exercised1 the power given him under the constitution of the United States to issue paper currency as the money of the nation. There was issued $450,000,000 of that currency, which was practically twice the total volume of the currency in issue at the commencement of the civil war. With national currency he found no difficulty in financing the successful prosecution of the greatest war that had been fought in history up to that time. Believing that one could follow with safety a statesman with the profound understanding and recognized genius that Lincoln possessed, I made bold to work out a programme which I published in 1935. May I take a moment to read just a page, as follows:
Lincoln fully appreciated that his national currency system -would not and could not of itself create or maintain stable prosperity. He recognized, however, that the establishment of a national currency system was the first step in any scheme designed to stabilize progress and to_ rationalize prosperity. Experience since Lincoln's time has taught us that in addition to the mint there are at least four administrative institutions that must be set up before progress financed with national currency and public credit monetized in a national banking 
system can be maintained with any substantial degree of economic and social security. These institutions constitute the basis of the five-point plan that is essential to the reestablishment of normal prosperity. The fundamental institutions making up this five-point plan consist of:
(1)	The Mint.
(2)	A national banking system.
(3)	An effective plan of scientific taxation.
(4)	A department of economic regulation and
control.
(5)	A department of international trade and
credit control.
Let me now summarize broadly the functions of these proposed governmental innovations, commencing with the Mint:
(1)	The Mint should mint, print and issue all metal and paper currency.
The time has gone by when a private corporation should print the bills for the bank of Canada.
(2)	National banking.
The national banking system should be empowered-
(a) To manage the gold and silver reserves of the nation; to control the minting, printing and issuing of all currency, including metal coins, paper bills, and bank credits which, when transferred by cheque, serve as a substitute for currency.
fb) To issue all the currency and credit requirements of the privately-owned and operated merchant or commercial banking system and to supervise and regulate the operation of all merchant and commercial banks.
(c)	To regulate and control all long-term capital investment, including investments such as advances for farm and home investments; all long-term industrial investments and all investments required for the expansion and development of international trade.
(d)	To regulate and control the nation's international buying power and all international currency and credit transactions.
(e)	To finance national, state, provincial and municipal government.
I then declared reasons why I shall vote against the amendment calling upon this house to nationalize the merchant banking system. Then I gave the same .reasons I now hold, when I wrote:
These proposals recognize that the creation and original issue of currency and credit as the spending power of government, the regulation of circulation, and the management of international exchange and credit are public functions that should be performed by departments of the national government. They also recognize that commercial or merchant banking is essentially a private enterprise that should be carried on by individuals operating in a private capacity but under proper government regulation and control.
There is no need for the nationalization of the merchant or commercial banlung system, nor should there be any attempt made to socialize private finance.
Mark what has happened since that was written. To-day we own the Bank of Canada,

The Budget-Mr. McGeer
and I am proud of the part that I had in making that institution the property of the people of the Dominion of Canada. To-day it has in its portfolios one billion dollars of dominion, government and provincial government securities. To-day it has in issue almost one billion dollars of Canadian paper currency -national currency issued by an institution owned by the people of Canada and serving in this war. Of course the Tories said to me in those days: That kind of thing was heresy. The former leader of the opposition, the member for York-Sunbury, was chairman of the banking and commerce committee the day I appeared before that body in 1934, and he remembers the attitude that was taken.
I then declared that we were in a war with poverty and that we should exercise the same powers to restore proper working conditions in Canada that we would be compelled to exercise were we threatened with aggression from abroad. I then declared to those who were claiming that "we could not finance by government spending to prosperity, that we could not lift ourselves by our own bootstraps, that all my ideas were the visionary things and the concepts of crackpots and funny money people, men who did not understand the fundamental bases of the higher realms of political economy"-I then declared that if war ever came we should find no difficulty in financing the cost, no matter how great it would be. Now the great lesson that we have learned in this war is the lesson that all the poverty and all the tragedy of unemployment and all of the demoralization of the dole came because we had followed the advice of leaders who were surrounded by advisers who did not know what they were talking about. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that in the course of my legal career I have examined a great many experts in many fields of activity, and I have always found that when expert opinion does not conform to plain reason and common sense you can be sure of one of two things: either the expert does not know what he is talking about, or he is deliberately fooling you.
I propose to offer to this parliament for its consideration in the way of recommendations to the government when we consider the budget resolutions some suggestions by which I believe we can greatly improve the war strength of the Dominion of Canada, some suggestions which if followed out and developed will give us a much greater power to meet with success the problems of reconstruction that are before us. Let me suggest this to members of this parliament who carry responsibility to-day not only for
financing this war but for carrying it through to a successful conclusion, and who have some responsibility to wage it in such a way that in the post-war period we shall emerge equipped to make this Canada of ours worthy of the men who have given so much, and who are giving more in this war than men have ever given in any other war that has ever been fought. We may secure, Mr. Speaker, all that is indicated by the Beveridge plan, and indicated in much wider degree in the plan proposed by the National Resources Planning Board of United States, indicated by our own Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), who is directing Canada's programme of rehabilitation, in great measure with the employment power of national currency. Such plans can be carried out with success if financed with national currency. But we cannot even approach them or carry them out with anything but disaster if we persist in depending only upon our power to issue unpayable national debt.
In conclusion I just want to say this. Let no one feel that we in Canada have as yet been called upon to make in this war any serious measure of sacrifice. If we will only appreciate the suffering and the sacrifices of the people of China and compare our position with theirs, if we will go through Stalingrad and Leningrad and into the area which was the home of more than fifty million Russian people, if we will go into any part of the devastated areas in Europe we cannot help but come to a realization that the full extent of our power of service is as yet far from reached. Yes, and let no one come to the conclusion that this war is being won in the factories of Canada. It is being won, as every war is won, by the men who are crusading in the air, the men who are fighting on the seas, the tank men and the artillery men and the infantrymen who are fighting on the land. Let us measure our efforts in the light of known sacrifices; and so guided we may in parliament prove worthy of the sacrifices and devotion to duty that are expressed in every field of action by our armed' services, then and then only we can look forward to having the men who are fighting and winning the war return with some little appreciation of our efforts.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow the arguments of the hon. member who has just spoken, except that I wish to thank him most sincerely on behalf of this group for the very kind tributes he paid to that great Progressive Conservative leader, Mr. The Budget-Mr. Homuth

Churchill. The leadership he is giving to England is the type of leadership which the people of Canada can expect from the Progressive Conservative party.
I had no intention of taking part in this debate, until two speeches were made this week in this house. The first was made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) the day before yesterday, and in the course of it he used these words as reported in Hansard, ~page 1470:
I may say in passing, that I should not like to have Colonel Drew's responsibility for explaining what he did in this great war, as a contribution to the winning of this war. He is a man trained as a soldier. So far as I know, he has not offered his services in any capacity of that kind.
I am sorry that the minister is not in his seat, because I want- to say this to him. I have not risen in my place in this house for the purpose of defending Colonel George Drew. Colonel Drew is well able to defend himself, as he has proved on more than one occasion. Were it not for the fact that the governmerit know his ability to defend himself, perhaps they might have gone much further than they did with the charges they laid against him under the defence of Canada regulations. But what I am defending, and what I intend to continue to defend and will always defend, is the right of any citizen of this country, any member of parliament, whether federal or provincial, to criticize this government and its acts without having his loyalty to Canada questioned.
The minister would seek to imply that only those who have offered their services in this war are entitled to criticize or, apparently, to play any part in the carrying on of this war. Well, at least I am in the happy position that even under that dictum I am able to criticize the government if I do so wish, because I did offer my services at the very beginning of the war, not as a dollar a year man or as one seeking any expenses; my services were offered free gratis to the former minister of national defence.
Be that as it may, suppose we should accept the dictum of the Minister of Munitions and Supply; suppose we should extend it, as we certainly could, if it is to be the measure of a man's right to criticize his government, and say that only those who fought or were in the armed services in the last war could serve in the government or be connected with it during the present war; were that principle to be applied, many hon. members now sitting in the cabinet and on the government side would not be there. I desire to express my 
condemnation of any such statement as that made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply.
At the beginning of this session the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) pleaded with us and with all hon. members to carry on this debate without rancour and without bitterness. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) pleaded the other day for cooperation. No government which has ever exercised power in this country has had greater cooperation from an opposition than this government has had. I think back to the years 1930 to 1935, when we were fighting, not a war with guns and tanks and planes, but one of the most disastrous economic wars which this country or this world ever saw. Go and read Hansard and see what sort of cooperation the government of that day received from hon. members who sat in the opposition at that time.

If the boorishness and the short temper which are being displayed by hon. gentlemen on the government benches are to be the measure of debate in this house, if that is what we are to expect as a gauge of battle on the various matters which come before this house, they can rest assured that we will accept that gauge of battle. Their boorishness does not fluster us, it does not scare us; we do not scare that easily; and I tell them here and now that if that sort of thing is to continue in this house, they can only expect the same sort of treatment from members of the opposition.
As I have said, the statement of the Minister of Munitions and Supply is one of the reasons why I rose at this time. Further, I feel that he was extremely discourteous to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) when he refused to allow him to ask a question. One's temper may be short at times; under great stress, perhaps, one says what he should not say, but discourtesy in this house is absolutely uncalled for.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and you had better begin to practise courtesy over there.
I am speaking in this debate to-day also because of the speech made on March 22 by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), in which he says, as reported in Hansard,-page 1439:
The reason is that ever since this session opened there has been a concerted campaign by the capitalist groups in this house and by the capitalist press outside it, to launch a storm of vilification and abuse at the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation.

The Budget-Mr. Homuth
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, speaking in the house a week or so ago, said that he was sick and1 tired of the lecturing he had received continually from the group to his left, and he resented it. I resent, and have resented ever since the house opened this session, the speeches made by hon. members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group in trying to paint a picture of other hon. members who do not belong to their group as men who are not sincere, not honest in their expressions of policy and in their representation of their people.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I do not think we have ever said that or implied that. We disagree with them fundamentally, but we have never implied a lack of sincerity or honesty. I hope my hon. friend will withdraw that statement.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The implication was there, if not expressed in words. It was an effort to build up in the minds of the people of this country the idea that even though we have enunciated in our policy certain things in which we believe, we cannot be trusted to carry them out; that no faith can be placed in what we say. That has been the sum and substance of nearly every Cooperative Commonwealth Federation speech made in this house this session.
There are hon. members in this house, in different parties, who have_ been reelected time after time, honoured with the votes of the people of their constituencies. Surely the people must have some faith in those men to return them election after election. I do not agree with many of the policies of hon. members on the government side, but I would be the last to suggest that they are not sincere in those policies. I have always felt that when a man offers himself for public office he does it with an honest desire to serve his people and better their condition. I resent this "holier than thou" attitude on the part of members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. We have heard nothing from hon. members of the socialist group except a tirade against the parties in this house which from the time of confederation have built up this country to what it is to-day. Speeches of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation inside and outside this house have no other purpose than to build up in the mind of the people an idea of the great righteousness of their cause and the cause of those who adhere to their party, and doubts as to the probity of those who do not.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) read letters painting a dismal picture of poverty and squalor in certain parts of this country. True there is poverty, and much of it can be and must be overcome. There is squalor, and much of it can be overcome with the betterment of conditions. But the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are going to bring in regimentation,
I suppose, and will say to everyone in this country: You must have a bathtub; you must have all the plumbing facilities in your house. Fine; they should have them. But is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation also going to say by legislation: You have to take a bath? Is it going to have peeping Toms going around to see that people do take a bath?
I think often of the story that has been told, and sometimes I believe there must be some foundation for it, of a man saying at a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation meeting: "If we get into power you will all have strawberries and cream." A man in the back of the hall said, "I don't like strawberries and cream." The speaker said, "It doesn't matter whether you like it or not; you are going to have it." Members might well be measured sometimes by the example they show in their own constituencies as to their right and qualification to hold public office. I look around this house at men who, it is said, will not carry out any progressive legislation if they should get into power. I think of hon. members of whose achievements I know something. I think of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) and the work he has done in his own district in building that monument, the Toronto East General hospital. I think of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who through all his public life has been known as the soldier's friend. During the last war not a troop train arrived at or left Toronto that he, as mayor of the city, was not there to meet or see off, to say a word of welcome or farewell. I think of how at any hour of the night, hearing that a train was coming with some wounded, he as mayor of the city was there to meet them. I think of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the work he has done for the British war victims' relief fund sponsored by the Toronto Telegram, and for the Toronto Star Red Cross fund. I think of the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Desmond), who long before he came to this house did such splendid work in organizing the tobacco growers and other producers in his district; the hon. member for Essex South (Mr. Clark), the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. MacKenzie)-the work they did of a
The Budget-Mr. Homuth

similar kind in their districts, and other hon. members too numerous to mention; men who really accomplished something back home. These are the men who, according to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation speakers, even though they have a very progressive platform, cannot be trusted to carry it out. The implication is that there is only one party that will fulfil its promises, and that is the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. They are doing everything possible to enlist support so that they can increase their numbers in this house or perhaps form a government. Their efforts remind me very much of someone two thousand years ago who went into the temple to pray and said, God, I thank Thee that I am not as other men are, or even as this publican.
My county is a little different from many others. It is settled by people from almost eveiy country in the world. I think of those old Scotch settlers who came from Dumfries and built one of the finest cities in Canada, the.city of Galt. I think of the hardships they went through, and I am happy to realize the prosperity they enjoy to-day and all that they have done to build up this country. I like to think of the Irish and English in my county who have done such good work. I think of the men of German birth who came here one hundred or one hundred and forty years ago to escape regimentation and militarism and find freedom under the British flag, and who did so much to build up this country. I think of the people who came from Pennsylvania, trekked through the swamps and settled in our part of the country, and the great work they have done to build up Canada, about whom the book "The Trail of the Conestoga" was written. I think of the many Ukrainian citizens, not only in my county but throughout this country, who are to-day ably represented in this house by the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Hlynka). I like to think of Canada not as a land of poverty and squalor but as a land of happy homes and prosperous farms, of developed water powers and industries. That is the picture I like to see. I see the boys and girls being educated under one of the finest school systems in the world1 and finding opportunity to make something of themselves, provided that they are prepared to put something of themselves into the job. They are not looking for some soft spot. We want them to have an opportunity to develop, and it is our responsibility to see that they have it. Surely this utopia that is being promised by certain speakers on platforms throughout the country is not the sort of life to which the boys and girls of this country are looking forward.

Then on several occasions another member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group seemed to be in great travail on account of the sending of beer to Libya. I interpret his efforts in that connection in two ways. In the first place we realize that, with the war on, there is in this country a body of public opinion-true, its strength is far more vocal than numerical-seeking to use the war as an excuse to bring about prohibition in Canada. The hon. member to whom I refer has frequently criticized the shipment of beer to Libya. I feel that this is a subtle attempt to get the support of the prohibition element of this country for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party when an election comes.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is imputing a motive to the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), which under the rules of this house he ought not to do.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then I withdraw it; it is said, but I withdraw it. However, in his efforts in this connection the hon. member has frequently mentioned the name of a man who holds a very high position with the allied governments, in an attempt to show that he had some influence which enabled him to obtain some preference in regard to shipping space in order that this beer might be sent to Libya, I am quite prepared to leave to the British high command the question of whether or not beer should go to the troops in Libya. I am quite prepared to leave it to their judgment as to whether or not the troops in Libya should have beer; and if they should have it, then for heaven's sake let us see that they get it. Think of those men driving tanks in that hell-hole of Libya and Tunisia; flying planes; fighting in the sandstorms, and all the rest of it! Surely the high command of Britain can be depended upon to do what they think is in the best interests of the warfare there. They will not buy beer from Canada simply to satisfy Mr. Taylor, who is the head of a brewing corporation. Let us have done with this sort of thing. If there are those members of this house who feel that we should have prohibition in Canada, let them rise in their places and move a resolution to that effect, and let the members of this house go on record as to how they stand on this whole question.
Then the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) delivered a speech in which reference was made to the men who are running the war effort of this country-the dollar-a-year men, the bankers, the capitalists and the industrialists. The hon. member would try to leave in the minds of the people of this

The Budget-Mr. Homuth
country the idea that these men are not there to help win the war; that they are not concerned with driving the vicious philosophy of nazism from this earth, but that they are there for only one purpose, namely, to gain wealth as a result of our war effort, to throw contracts and rewards to the companies with which they were connected. I have had a great deal to do with many of these men. It is true that there are some instances of square pegs in round holes; that can happen when thousands upon thousands of men are being hired. I should like to see that changed; I should like to see every man fit into his job. But I know these men, and I know the work they are doing. I know that many of them work seven days a week, and long hours every day. These men are concerned with winning this war, because they know as well as anyone knows that if we lose this war nothing w7e have will matter. So that I resent any attempt to build up in the minds of the Canadian people a distrust of the men who in their own way are doing the best they can. Certainly there may be room for improvement, but let us not try to make the people of this country feel that anyone who happens to be connected with industry or with financial institutions is taking part in the war effort for only one purpose, namely, to better the financial position of himself and his friends.
Then we find a campaign being carried on by the Committee of Industrial Organization and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in collaboration. In organizing their unions the Committee of Industrial Organization seem to be more concerned with calling meetings at which they have Cooperative Commonwealth Federation political speakers; and to me their concern seems to be much greater for the future of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party than for the welfare of the industrial workers whom they are trying to organize. I have seen a good deal of this. I have seen some instances of it in my own riding. I will speak about them in a few moments. I know something about the labour movement. I have been closely associated with it throughout my political life, during which I have always fought for those things for which the trade unions stand. Apparently some of the unions have pledged their support to Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidates. Not only are the Committee of Industrial Organization organizers trying to urge the working men to support the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidates; if they get sufficiently powerful they will force the working men to do so, and they are doing their utmost to take from the working men the most sacred freedom we
have in this or any other democratic country, namely, the freedom and secrecy of the ballot. The very success of the trade union movement in the old country has been due to the fact that it never became a political party.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh. It is true that the heads of trade unions are part and1 parcel of the Labour party in Britain, but the unions as such are not mixed up with that party. The day that trade unions in this country enter politics as unions, that day the trade unions will die. However, realizing what is the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, one can readily appreciate that if they got into power and had the right to bring about the regimentation which they are urging, then there would be no need for trade unions; trade unions would die, as they have died in Germany, Italy and other countries.
I should like now to give the house a few instances of the methods the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are using to build up their party, for these are methods to which I do not think the Canadian people are going to take very kindly. I now mention a personal matter, because a denial through the newspapers would be of no avail. The lie has already gone out. I want to show the type of campaign these people are carrying on. In the present instance there was some difficulty in some of the factories in Waterloo South. A large meeting w'as called, and was held in the theatre in Galt. The meeting was well advertised-I hold the advertisement in my hand-as a meeting of the organized steel workers of Galt and district. The fact of the matter is that there was no organization at that meeting. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) was there as guest speaker. The whole sum and substance of the meeting was the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and the need for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in this company's operations.

speechtext:
During the course of the meeting one of the smaller fry in the organization, one who is there as a Committee of Industrial Organization organizer, made a statement concerning myself and Mr. Hipel, Minister of Labour and Public Welfare in the Ontario legislature. There had been some difficulty in the plant of the Butler Stampings and Machine Screws company at Preston. That company came to our town about four years ago. We then had two
The Budget-Mr. Homuth

empty factory buildings. Mr. Hipel and I, along with many other citizens, took an active part in bringing that company to the town, with the result that to-day they are employing three or four hundred hands. They are occupying those factories, and doing a great job in the war effort.
However, during the course of the meeting the man Williams, rising from his seat, said: "The only reason we cannot expect any consideration or assistance from the two members for this constituency is that they are- both shareholders andl directors of the Butler company." He knew that statement was a deliberate lie; but it was a sample of the type of malicious propaganda that is being carried on throughout this country, in order to bolster up the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. That was a lie. Neither of us had any financial interest in the company. Our only interest was to bring a new industry into the district, and we were successful in doing so. But that is typical of the kind of campaign being carried on.
It is not confined to the smaller fry in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. According to the Weyburn Review, after Mr. Meighen had1 become leader of this group the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation made a speech at Weyburn. These were the words he used: "I would rather live under Hitler than under Meighen."

speechtext:
-but I do wish to say that there never was -a time in the history of our country when we should be more active in developing a spirit of trust among all the various factions who go to make up our population. We must deal with that problem in a country so vast, and with such a small population, a country with so tremendous a future ahead1 of it. With careful planning and careful working out of such plans, this country has fifty or a hundred years of prosperity ahead of it. These things can be ours. This future can be the future of our children and of our children's children if we are prepared in all parts of this dominion to give and take when dealing with these matters. There can be no east or no west; there can be no Ontario or no Quebec; there must be just Canada. That is what we must have. There must be that spirit of give and take; we must be willing to give more and take less.
If we build upon that foundation we have nothing whatever to fear. But you cannot build as the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is trying to build to-day. You cannot build by trying to create distrust by one faction of another. You cannot build by
creating the feeling that one faction is right and the other is wrong, by talking against the general welfare of this country. That is not the foundation upon which we want to build Canada. It is certainly not the situation as it exists in Canada to-day. When they paint that picture, they paint a picture that is not true. These hon. gentlemen have painted certain word pictures in this house about conditions in Canada and about the type of men who are running this country. When the man overseas reads these dispatches he cannot help wondering what is going on in Canada. So that I say: Let us as Canadians make up our minds that there is only one thing we are concerned about, the building up of a happy future for those men who are doing such a good job in defending this country and who will continue to defend it as long as the war continues, and for those children who are now growing up and who are deserving of a splendid future.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to say that I like the spirit displayed by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) in delivering his speech. Whenever he speaks he puts forth the utmost of his energies, and that is what makes him so interesting, as can be judged by the applause from both sides of the house. Following the two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me, I find myself in a iposition. similar to that of a young man who was run over by a car. When the doctor examined him and saw there was little hope, he asked the unfortunate man if he were married. The young man said, "No, this is the worst fix I have ever been in." Following two such brilliant speakers, I find myself in a similar position. Nevertheless, I should like to bring to the attention of the government and the members of the house a few of the problems which I believe face us to-day or will face us in the near future. One problem is the victory loan campaign, and the other is the shortage of farm labour which faces the farmers of Canada, particularly those of western Canada. I believe something should be done to assist those people in meeting their problems and so that they may do their part in Canada's-war effort.
During the last two years we have heard a great deal in Canada about the many charters and about the various freedoms which are promised to the people of this country and to those of the allied nations, and perhaps to the people of the other countries of the world when the war is over. As a member representing a farming constituency, I wish to place before this house the views of my people who are deeply interested in all charters
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

that will guarantee security to our nation and in freedoms that will guarantee security to every individual in this dominion. In addition, the farmers of my constituency and, I believe, most farmers of Canada are interested in more freedoms.
The President of the United States announced only four freedoms, but I found that I could not condense the freedoms wanted by the farmers into less than eight. The farmers of Canada want, first, freedom from fear of the sheriff and financial institutions. Second, they want freedom from thousands of orders in council and the bureaucracy which has [DOT]grown up. Third, they want freedom from incompetency and mismanagement of people's -affairs. Fourth, they want freedom from amfulfilled promises made for political reasons only. Fifth, they want freedom from crushing taxation upon those in the lower income brackets. Sixth, they want freedom from fear and want in the midst of plenty. Seventh, they want freedom from those who thrive by keeping people in misery. Eighth, they want freedom from confusion. It seems to me that there is more confusion in Canada than is good for us. Many of the problems facing the Canadian people are not as bad as they appear to be on the surface, but the confusion that exists makes them appear much worse than they really are. Can we not approach these problems by first removing some of this confusion?
I have received a number of letters from the headquarters of the victory loan campaign in Edmonton and Calgary asking me as a member of the house to assist them in putting *over the campaign. I am sure that hon. members know the stand of this group on -victory loan campaigns. At all times we are only too anxious to assist the government in its campaigns, even though we do not agree with the manner in which the government is financing most of its expenditures. As one of the members of this group I wish at all times to assist the government in whatever way I can and may. I have done so during the past three sessions and shall continue to do so, particularly in connection with the larger problems that are facing our nation.
May I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to the attention of the house the fact that I have actually seen farmers in my constituency weeping when they could not afford to buy victory bonds or war savings certificates. I have seen men of fifty, sixty and seventy years of age most despondent because they were not in a position to buy bonds and certificates. One particular farmer told me that he had to meet a mortgage obligation within

fifteen days, and that if he did not do so the mortgage company would foreclose. He said to me, " How can I possibly help Canada in this victory loan campaign if my own home and everything I have toiled for during the past fifty years will be taken away from me if I do not meet this mortgage payment?" He went on to say, " The quota on wheat deliveries is so low that I cannot possibly meet this payment, and yet if my district does not reach its quota in this victory loan it will be branded as not being loyal to Canada and to our cause in this war." If the government is concerned about these farmers and about placing them in a position so that they may be able to purchase victory bonds, the mortgage companies should be told-no, a measure should be passed by this house forbidding the collection of private farm debts now and cancelling all interest arrears. Then the farmer would be in a position to purchase victory bonds with the money which he would otherwise use to meet his debt obligations, and after the war he would be in a position to cash 'his bonds and pay off his contractual obligations, which seem to be so sacred to this. government. That is the only way in which we can make it possible for every farmer to buy victory bonds and war saving certificates, and I commend that suggestion to the government.
I have come to the conclusion, after the three sessions that I have sat in this house, that many hon. members really do not understand conditions in the west. It is not that they are not honest or do not mean well, but they simply do not understand the conditions of the western farmer. They have perhaps never seen an elderly gentleman of sixty-five or seventy years of age weeping because he has been dispossessed of his land and home. But that is a spectacle that may be seen right across the western provinces, and among these farmers will be found the finest type of pioneers that this country has ever had, men who have been toiling for years, clearing the land and building their homes and bringing up their families, men who in reality have been the builders of this nation and who should be entitled to some reward instead of being turned out of their homes. But what do they get? The heartless mortgage company walks in and tells the farmer to get out or the consequences will be worse for him-they will put him in gaol if he does not. After living among these people for many years and travelling throughout the country, I know that these are not men who squandered their incomes on things they did not need. They have not lived a

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka
life that does not entitle them to save something at least from their labours. They have done their very best. In this connection I should like to quote a few figures taken from Farm Forum Facts, a non-political publication published in Toronto. It quotes figures from the bureau of statistics for 1931 and 1936 showing that the tenancy of land in Canada is gradually passing from private individual owners to mortgage companies. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, the census of 1941 was taken two years ago, and we have not as yet been given the figures showing the trend in more recent years. I ask why? The figures may be so appalling, so frightening to the people of Canada that no government would be able to justify itself in permitting such conditions to continue or for allowing them to come about. The figures for 1931 show that Nova Scotia had the highest number of owned, mortgage-free farms, with about 85 per cent of her farms being in that group; New Brunswick had 77 per cent mortgage-free; Quebec, 63 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 62 per cent; British Columbia, 60 per cent; Ontario 48 per cent; Alberta, 44 per cent; Manitoba, 42 per cent; and Saskatchewan, about 36 per cent. Will anyone suggest to me that these farmers have not done their best to meet their debt obligations out of the meagre income they have received from their produce, and that is the only income they have because they have no side-line of any kind? Will any one say that this is a happy state of affairs? The hon. member for Waterloo-South said in his address this afternoon that he would like to see this a land of happy homes. Every honest Canadian would like to see Canada a land of happy homes. We cannot, however, have happy homes while mortgages cover the properties of our pioneers right across the country. Let me quote further from this publication:
The trend away from farm ownership continued in the years following 1931. No statistics will be available to show this trend for the whole of Canada, until the 1941 census has been compiled. But the trend, as revealed by the 1936 prairie census, is marked.
There the number of fully owned, mortgage-free farms had declined, by 1936, to 24 per cent of the total; the number of owned, mortgaged farms had risen to 40 per cent; the number of farmers renting rose to 19 per cent, and the number of partly owned, partly rented farms rose to about 17 per cent.
Here is another quotation from the same article:
Fall in Value
The value of the farm property actually owned by the farmers fell from 56 per cent to 40 per cent, while the value held by landlords rose from 28 to 34 per cent, and that held by mortgagees from 16 to 26 per cent.
The point I wish to make here, and with which I am sure there will be a general agreement, is that when the returns from the 1941 census are available it will be shown that fewer than half the farmers of western Canada own their homes. Fewer than half have any say as to the wealth they produce. Where are we going? Whither are we drifting? It will be seen that within the next five to ten years, mortgage companies and other financial institutions will operate farms in large units and will be in competition with the farmers of western Canada in regard to the price on wheat and other products which are raised by the farmers. Then an individual farmer will not be able to exist, because it will not be possible for him to compete. This is a trend which has been permitted to continue now for more than twelve years, and it should be stopped. If our farmers are dispossessed of their properties and are allowed to work only as tenants, the consequences to Canada would be really terrible. We would lose the creative genius which has characterized the country's pioneers.
Let me for a moment draw attention to the incomes of our farmers. I have here a publication of the Canadian federation of agriculture showing farm incomes in percentages compared with those of other groups. Remember that one-third of the total population in Canada is engaged in agriculture, so that it would be * logical to expect that the farmers would receive one-third of the total national income, and that would mean parity prices, and that is how it should be. But here are the facts:
