And so down the line until 1940, in which year the percentage, instead of being 33-3 per cent was 11-0 per cent. I have not the figures for 1941 and 1942, but it is certain that the percentage will not be one-third; indeed, I am certain that it will be less than half that figure.
How then can the farmer meet his obligations? How can he be expected' to pay his debts, buy victory bonds, clothe and feed his children and send' them to school, and pay his hospital and doctor bills? I do not care what sort of picture is painted about the prices the farmers are getting for their hogs, honey and other commodities; so long as the farmers are not receiving one-third of the national income, someone else is getting it.
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

I will now turn to the subject of grading of live stock and point out what seems to me to be a ridiculous situation. I have here a clipping which was sent to me by one of my constituents, who a^ks, "Will you ask the government to explain why a situation of this sort exists?" This clipping is taken, I believe, from the Edmonton Journal, and states:
Note: new cuts on heavies, $3 per carcass discount; extra heavies $2 per cwt. discount; redglings $5 each discount.	.
Here is a letter to the editor of the same newspaper and on the same subject: Inconsistency
Sir-Have just finished listening to a radio announcer exhorting the housewives of Canada to save fats, and he wound up his plea with the statement that "10 pounds of fat would provide explosive for 29 anti-aircraft shells." A commendable plea, doubtless instigated by the federal government, but the government's plea to save fats, badly needed for explosives, and the statement of my hog returns which I have in my pocket do not make sense. These returns for hogs for the week of Jan. 12, 1913, state: "One heavy, 188 pounds (two pounds overweight, deduction or penalty $1.88) % Return for Jan. 19, one heavy, 192 pounds (six pounds overweight, deduction $2.88)." Therefore, I was penalized $4.76 for producing eight pounds of fat too much. Will the consumer receive the benefit of this $4.76 deduction? . . .
We know the old argument that "our standards must be maintained to retain the British market after the war", but haven't we been told there is an emergency and to increase pork production? And also that the meat ration per person for the civilian population of England is four ounces per week? Me thinks the British consumer *would be pleased to get a litle extra fat.
If the federal government allowed the Canadian farmer to put another twenty pounds on each hog we farmers would produce more fat for explosives in a month than the housewives of this country could save in six years.
There may be something rotten in the state of Denmark, but we hog producers are convinced there is something definitely rotten in the hog grading system in the state of Canada. The inconsistency of the government's pleas and their actions in this regard rouses a strong feeling of disgust.-Yours, H. R. Boutillier.

speechtext:
The hon. member at all times wants to paint a picture before this house showing the enviable position of the farmer. He may be one of the prosperous farmers, but he must remember that he has a sideline, being a member of this house. Thousands of farmers in my constituency have no income other than the farm income. I am trying to point out the conditions under which they exist. I should be glad to discuss with the hon. member his point of view, but I think we can do so somewhere else and not take up my time here.
The income of the farmer is only one phase of the problem. We may point out that the farmer is getting a little more for his hogs, for his cream and for other commodities, but we must take into consideration other things such as the freight the farmer of western Canada must pay on everything he buys from Ontario and Quebec, and on everything he sells as well, and has to ship east of Edmonton or Saskatoon or Winnipeg. He must pay the freight .both ways. The farmer is the only person in Canada who has to do that. Why should it be permitted? Why should not the manufacturer in the east say, all right, I will pay the freight on my binder because I am selling it to the farmer in Alberta, and the farmer in Alberta will pay freight on his wheat. But no, the farmer has to bear the cost both ways. It is ridiculous. Candidates of the government party have been campaigning for years in western Canada promising the farmer that the freight rate structure will be overhauled. But there has not been a move made in that direction.

Let us consider another problem that faces the farmer. At the present time the implement companies have closed the little shops they had in the outlying towns for the sale of farm machinery parts. If today the farmer needs something for his tractor or binder, he has to get out his car, use rubber and gas that should be saved, and go fifteen or twenty or more miles, and every farmer has to do the same. That is a mistake. The government should make it possible for the farmers to have these parts available within walking distance or a horseback ride. I know farmers sixty or seventy miles from Edmonton who have to make a trip to get a little gadget

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka
for the binder. In the same connection there may be some small part broken that might cost only 25 cents, but the machine company says, You cannot get that little part; you must buy the whole thing, and you must pay $5 for it. The farmer has nothing to say; he must hand in the old piece of machinery to get the new piece. Who gets the benefit? All the company has to do is to adjust the piece handed in and sell it again for five dollars. That is absolutely unfair.

speechtext:
In the five minutes left at my disposal, Mr. Speaker, I should like to touch on the shortage of farm labour. In the first place, agriculture must.definitely be considered an essential war industry; then, that being so, postponements should be granted more readily to farmers and farmers' sons. In practice the onus of proof rests upon the applicant. I know many young men in my constituency who were called up and who applied for postponements, but were either refused or granted postponements too
short to enable them to get rid of their stock. So that many of these young men left everything standing as it was and went into the service. The country loses a great deal by hurried decisions of that kind. I suggest that many men in the service to-day should be granted leave for two weeks, six weeks or whatever time may be necessary in order that they may get rid of their stock and settle their affairs.
That is the first thing that must be done. Then I believe it is essential that we standardize the form of these applications for postponement. I know many young men have had legitimate cases for postponement; but because they were not able to word their applications as well as some others, their requests were refused. Another chap may be a bit shrewder; his application may perhaps be more attractive or his request presented in a better form, so that while his case may not be as worthy of consideration as that of the other chap, his application may be granted1.
There are two other points I should like to mention in this connection. The first is with regard to private debts of soldiers. I have a number of letters in my office from young men who tell me that mortgage companies are threatening to foreclose upon their land while they are away at war. That is unfair. There should not be a single foreclosure on the property of any man who happens to be defending this country, as well as the mortgage companies. I wish to bring that point to the attention of this house as forcibly as I can. In addition, the interest is accumulating on the debts of these men. That should not be the case. No one should expect interest on a debt owed by a soldier while he is away in the service of his country.
My time is slipping away rapidly, but my last point is that many of these young men were given only eight days in which to apply for a postponement, and if they failed to have their applications before the board within that time, their cases were not even heard or reviewed. Even to-day these cases should be reviewed, and they should be given an opportunity to apply for a leave to enable them to go home, dispose of their stock and make any arrangements necessary. I have received from my constituency many appeals which I have referred to the Department of National Defence. Most of them are hurriedly brushed aside, the answer I usually get being that the application has been refused, and that is the end of it. A board of appeal under the Department of National Defence should be set up in order that these cases may have a fair hearing when they are brought up.

The Budget-Mr. Maelnnis

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak in this debate, since I felt that anything I had to say on the budget could be said during the discussion of the resolutions. However, so much has been said during this debate in regard to the programme, the aims, the policies and the social philosophy of this group that at times I was not sure whether the budget had been introduced by the Minister of Finance or by some member from this comer of the house. I will try to reply to some of the statements that have been made and to bring some light into dark comers. Perhaps it is a waste of time. I hear the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) laughing; I imagine he realizes the futility of what I intend to try to do. However, I shall try to do it, regardless of the fact that I am aware that none are so blind as those who will not see or so deaf as those who will not hear.
I shall deal first with the former leader of the opposition, the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). In the course of his speech the other day he said that this group, this party, was spreading the gospel of hate throughout the country. Well, if I talked with such venom when I spoke about the Tory party as he does when he talks about the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, I should be inclined to agree with him. Speaking on March 18, he is reported at page 1358 of Hansard as follows:
The system of free enterprise may have been exploited and abused, if you will. I admit that. But with all its abuses it is a far better system than government regimentation and national socialism. What does it mean? What is the ultimate aim of national socialism? Well, it is fascism.	_
Mr. Douglas (Weyburn) : There is no national socialism in this country.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): They can deny it, but I can see as far through a stone wall as anybody.
I do not doubt the ability of my hon. friend to see through a stone wall as far as anybody. But his difficulty is that when he is playing politics, as he usually is in the house, he can see just as far through a stone wall as he can through a telescope.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now, isn't that clever?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When my hon. friend
applies the appellation of national socialism to the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation he is doing what he knows to be incorrect, or he does not know the difference between national socialism and democratic socialism.
I would draw the attention of the house to the fact that Hitler's national socialism did not

seem so abhorrent to my hon. friends a few years ago. May I read to the house the eulogy of the leader of national socialism in Germany made in this house by a former leader of the Conservative party, Doctor R. J. Manion. This is what he said on September 8, 1939, as reported at page 14 of Hansard for the special war session:
But, sir, Germany is controlled at the present time by an unscrupulous egoist. It is true he served Germany well, and had he stopped at a certain point he might well have gone down into history as a great German hero. He raised the German people from discouragement, gave them back their pride after a just but humiliating defeat. Had he stopped there he would have been accepted perhaps by all the world as a German hero. But he did not stop there.
Yes, he would have been accepted by people with minds like my hon. friend; but he would not have been accepted by socialists anywhere in the world as a German hero. He would have been accepted as the gangster that he is.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are a little late in your denunciation.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants to read the record he will find my denunciation of nazism clear and sound from the very beginning.
What I have quoted represents the attitude of all Conservative-minded people. I have in my hand another statement by another Conservative-not in this country. This was the man sent from Great Britain in a last effort to appease Hitler. I refer to the late Sir Nevile Henderson, ambassador to Germany from 1937 to the beginning of the war. Upon his return to Great Britain he wrote a book entitled " Failure of a Mission." One would think that he and Doctor Manion had agreed between them as to what they wished to say. Sir Nevile Henderson said:
Nor are all dictatorships, even if prolonged, reprehensible.
Only communist dictatorships are reprehensible to Conservatives.
One cannot, just because he is a dictator, refuse to admit the great services which Signor Mussolini has rendered to Italy-
This is the man Churchill called a jackal, -nor would the world have failed to acclaim Hitler as a great German if- he had known when and where to stop-
If he had known enough to stop before he began to attack us, or before he became dangerous to our interests, he would have been a great man. But he did not stop there. I quote further:
. . . if for instance after Munich and the Nuremberg decrees for the Jews.

The Budget-Mr. Maelnnis
Doctor Manion and Sir Nevile Henderson were still willing to acclaim Hitler a great hero, despite the fact that he had ground a large section of the German population into the dust, and subjected the rest to the worst dictatorship the world had ever known.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And what about trade unions?
Mr. MaeINNIS: And he destroyed trade unionism; I am coming to that.
So long as Hitler was suppressing trade unions, destroying cooperatives, and imprisoning and shooting socialists, no fault was found with him by -my Conservative friends. This is what they used to say when they were among themselves-"Great Fellow, this Hitler -a little crude, maybe; but he certainly knows how to handle those dirty trade unionists. I wish we had someone here who had the guts to deal with our agitators in the same way." That was their attitude, and that is why we are fighting a war.
Where is the man in this house, either on the Conservative or the Liberal side, who protested or raised his voice when Hitler and Mussolini joined to force fascism on the Spanish people? There is no such man. We placed an embargo on Spain to prevent her from defending herself, and we shipped all the materials of war Hitler and Mussolini required.
Not only does the hon. member for York-Sunbury speak in the house about the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, but outside the house we are the theme of his every speech. He cannot get us off his mind. I feel somewhat encouraged by that fact. There is another thing that encourages me, also, that is that the more he talks the more our position improves.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are both happy, then; let us leave it at that.
Mr. MaeINNIS: No, I am not going to leave it at that. This is what the hon. member said when he spoke at the Progressive Conservative association dinner on March 13, according to a report in the Ottawa Citizen:
Mr. Hanson in his address said post-war plans were necessary, but the greatest struggle for survival was raging, and to win it should be the first consideration. "We have a long way to go yet and the people of Canada have many sacrifices to make," he said.
Mr. Hanson said the trouble wTith Canada's war effort was lack of national leadership. The prime purpose and objective of Prime Minister Mackenzie King was to maintain the solidarity and power of the Liberal party. The Prime Minister had entered the war with a policy of "moderate" participation, said Mr. Hanson,
and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation had declared against sending an expeditionary force overseas.
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party was striving not to win the war "but to win the next general election" and was "holding out the bribe" of nationalization of big industries.
I wonder what my hon. friend was doing when he made that speech? Was he trying to win the next general election? I think that is the purpose of most of his speeches. But do hon. members note the superiority?- everyone is out of step but our Dick. I hate to put a stain on the lily-white record he thinks he has, but I must say that if there is any one man in or out of the house who has consistently played politics since May 16, 1940, that man is the hon. member for York-Sunbury.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to page the Prime Minister on that point.
Mr. MaeINNIS: You can share the honours between you. I will go on a little further and show what my hon. friends have been doing for the last year and a half. I had not intended to speak of this because there is more important work at hand. But I wonder why the Conservative party is doing these things. Is it to win the next general election, or to lose it? Some of their actions seem to indicate that the purpose is to lose it.
About November, 1941, the National Conservatives held a conference in Ottawa, the purpose of which was to select a leader. Rightly or wrongly, of all the prominent public men in this country they selected the man most detested by labour. Writing to friends in Toronto when it became evident that this man was to be the new leader and saying that the action of the party in selecting Mr. Meighen seemed to me like the action of an organism that wanted to die but shrank from sudden death. It took the York South by-election to convince them of their mistake. Remember, they were not sorry because of the type of man they had selected; they were merely sorry because they had made a mistake. It took another little affair to really put the-I was just about to say something that would not be parliamentary-fear into them. On July 25, 1942, an informal labour conference took place in Toronto. This conference passed the following resolution.
Be it resolved that we believe and affirm that organized labour will be doing itself a great service and hastening the realization of its aims by entering into affiliation for political action with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation at the earliest possible moment, and that until such affiliation is an accomplished
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

fact, this conference calls upon all unions to endorse the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation as the official political arm of the trade union movement in Canada.
I wish to tell this house as a man who has been connected with organized labour for more than thirty years that that is the best day's work that organized labour did for itself during that time.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just a moment, now. The results were swift and they were impressive. Organized labour had been asldng the province of Ontario for a trade union bill for years. Two weeks after that resolution was passed, Peter Heenan, the minister of labour in the government of Ontario, said that there would be a trade union bill. Mr. Conant said a little later that a special session would be called to put through a trade union bill. That was before they had heard from Ontario employers. The resolution also had quite an effect upon a gentleman known as Mitchell Hepburn, one-time premier of Ontario, one-time friend of the Prime Minister of Canada, an all-time hater of organized labour. Overnight Mitchell Hepburn became the champion of civil liberties. In fact, one could see Mitch standing on the steps of Toronto gaols embracing communists or alleged communists as the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) released them.
Shortly after that labour conference the Conservatives decided to hold an informal conference and with due regard for the general fitness of things, they decided to hold it at Port Hope. Another thing they did, the first glimmering of intelligence I have noted in the Conservative party for the past thirteen years, was to exclude Conservative members of parliament from the conference. They did another thing that indicated growing intelligence. One of the members of their brain trust-I shall not mention his name, but there are not so many-borrowed from a friend of mine a book entitled "Social Planning for Canada" and took it to Port Hope to see if they could not get some ideas or inspiration out of it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the book "Liberal Way"?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The party who had the book "Liberal Way" were not going the Liberal way. Therefore the Conservatives decided that book would not do and they got something else. To come back for a moment to the conference held in Ottawa in 1941: As I said, they selected a leader who was to

be the pillar of fire that would lead them into the promised land of political power. But the pillar of fire of 1941 became the incubus of 1942, so that when they met at Winnipeg he was thrown out the window. They then proceeded to select a new leader and a new name. However, it should be noted that the new name depended upon the new leader. If N was to be the new leader, the name would be national Conservative party; if P was to be the new leader, the name would be Progressive Conservative party. That is how they came by the new name.
May I remind the members of this house that the aims and policies and even the social philosophy of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and of this group are not something that is particularly and peculiarly ours. Our policies are similar to those of labour parties in the other parts of the British commonwealth, such as Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand, and they are the same as the policies of democratic socialists no matter where they are found throughout the world. Therefore, when my hon. friends cast aspersions on the members of this group they are casting aspersions not only on this group but on men like Walter Nash, former minister of finance in the Labour government in New Zealand; they are casting aspersions on men like Herbert Morrison, member of the British war cabinet; they are casting aspersions on men like John Curtin, Prime Minister of Australia; they are casting aspersions on men like Sir Stafford Cripps, a member of the British war cabinet. In fact, Mr. Speaker, they are casting aspersions on scores of statesmen throughout the British empire, men without whom the world would be very much the poorer and its hope for the future very much darker.
I wish to say to this house that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is closely associated with the British Labour party and with the Labour party of Australia and New Zealand. I have in my hand a copy of a letter which was considered at an executive meeting of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation on September 19, 1942. The letter is dated from London, August 25, and is addressed to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It reads:
My dear Coldwell,
In the course of his address to our annual conference at Whitsuntide, the Rt. Hon. Dr. Evatt, a member of the Australian Commonwealth government said:
"If we are to progress together one thing is plain, and I ask you to consider it. The present relations between the labour organizations of

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
the British commonwealth of nations must become more intimate. It is only right and proper that the labour movements in all British countries should plan for the future together. I hope that steps to establish a closer liaison will be taken by you and taken soon."
Our national executive committee have expressed their agreement with the principle of holding a British commonwealth labour conference of the political labour parties in the British commonwealth and would welcome any proposals from your executive committee with regard to the time, place, composition and agenda of such a conference, and any other relevant observations or material, before taking any decisions in detail. We hope that your executive committee will give this matter their earnest consideration.
Yours sincerely,
William Gillies,
Secretary,
International Department, of the British Labour Party.
I wish to say a few words now about a matter which was raised by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) on Tuesday evening in this house. If talking to my friends to my right is a waste of time, I presume that talking for the benefit of the hon. member for Temiscouata is doubly so. In any event the hon. member for Temiscouata issued a challenge to this group to define profit and to teH the house how we could get along if no one made a profit. Then he gave his own definition of profit. He said:
When a man works hard for a few dollars a day, lives within his means and succeeds in saving perhaps a dollar or two each day, and then puts it in a bank or buys insurance with it, that is a profit, and it is a legitimate profit.
The hon. member for Temiscouata may have his own ideas of what is profit and what is legitimate profit. But the instance he gave is not profit. The man received a wage for a commodity sold-his labour power. When we talk about profit or profits I imagine we are using those words in their economic sense. I heard the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Iiinley), I think it was, say the other day that the flowers of the field made a profit. My understanding is that the lilies of the field toil not, neither do they spin, and consequently they do not make a profit for themselves or for anybody else. But for the benefit of the hon. member for Temiscouata I should like to give a definition of profit from "Webster's New International Dictionary," which defines profit as:
The share of the employing classes in the distribution of the product of industry, as distinct from wages which constitute the share of the labouring classes, and rent which constitutes the share of the landlord classes.
That is a proper definition of profit in political-economic terms. But if the hon. member for Temiscouata desires to get a clearer understanding of what profit really is, I would suggest that he read the report of the royal commission on price spreads in 1935. At page 115 of that report he will find the question of wages and profits in the tobacco industry dealt with. I quote from page 115:
The most striking fact revealed by our evidence on the tobacco industry is the combination of low wages and high profits.
In 1930, the average annual earnings of the workers in this industry, $662, were the third lowest in the forty industries for which the dominion bureau of statistics published data. Since that date, they have declined to as low as $555, which can be attributed to a 17 per cent decrease in the volume of employment and to a decrease in basic wage rates.
I quote again-:
Certain figures for the Imperial Tobacco Company, which is by far the largest single unit in this industry, are of special interest. In 1931, net profits were $5,914,079 and factory payrolls were $3,430,952, or 58 per cent of net profits; in 1933, factory payrolls totalled only 52 per cent of net profits.
In the Macdonald Tobacco Company, undivided profits at the end of 1933 stood at $594,432, notwithstanding the withdrawal of $260,000 annually by the president since 1930.
May I point out that at the rate of wages prevailing in 1933, $555, an employee of that company would have to work for 468 years before he would take out as much in wages as the president took out in one year. So that, if my hon. friend the member for Temiscouata cannot now understand the difference between wages and profits, the fault is not mine.
That was the condition found in 1935, and there have been no curbs applied and no changes made since, except for what may have happened since the war began. That is the condition which will prevail as soon as normal times return unless we find some way of curbing it. That is the profit system. That is free enterprise. It is what we object to, and I am satisfied that it is what an increasing number of people in this country are beginning to object to, as well.
I should like to develop that a little further because it is an interesting point; however, my time will not allow. But further information is very easily obtainable.
I said that I did not want to take part in this sort of debate, but I want my hoc. friends to know that if they desire a fight of this kind they can have it at any time they like.
I am sure that no man who has any understanding of the tremendous problems-military, social, political, racial, and a hundred

The Budget-Mr. LaCroix

and one others-which confront the world today, and will very likely confront it in an intensified way after the war, can deal lightly or carelessly with such issues.
Just a closing word. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation is the result of the social and economic developments in this country so far. Its roots are deep in the soil of Canada. Its growth cannot be stopped oy railing or misrepresentation. The only way in which it can be stopped is if some other party does the things we are advocating. Our aims and our policies are in tune with the times, and they will prevail.
Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Quebec-Mont-morency) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, everyone admits, I believe, that we shall come out of this war with a public debt of at least $15,000,000,000, for the interest on which we shall have to pay every year about $400,000,000. After the war we shall be unable to balance our budget without a deficit, without new loans or, still, without levying heavy taxes at a time when the national income will be considerably reduced. In fact, we shall then have to enforce a new social security legislation, and in the estimation of Professor Marsh, the cost of that social security plan,-which will necessarily have to be carried out,-will alone amount to about $900,000,000.
Everyone admits that the ceiling has been reached as regards taxes, at least in the case of wage-earners, because the tax which the latter have to pay at the source is higher in Canada than in the United States or England. Some will say "Why should we pay $400,000,000 a year for interest on a debt which will amount to about $15,000,000,000?" In reply I may say that I sincerely believe it is possible to eliminate those huge interest payments and lighten by a like amount the tax levied from wage-earners, especially those in the lower and medium brackets, who form the mass of our population and whose burden will necessarily have to be lightened if most of them are not to become, after the war, an even greater charge upon the government.
Why not put to greater use our Bank of Canada, instead of borrowing from the chartered banks and the public? The honourable the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) has stated in his budget speech that he had borrowed from the chartered banks only inasmuch as such loans were essential to meet our war expenditures. I blame the Minister of Finance for having overlooked the government's sovereignty in currency matters when he applied to chartered banks and the public instead of dealing solely with the Bank of Canada.
IMr. Maclnnis.]
It may be objected that loans from the Bank of Canada would be more harmful than loans from the chartered banks. What difference is there between a Bank of Canada note and a dominion bond?
A Bank of Canada note is a- promise on the part of the government or of its'bank,-which means the same thing-to pay to the bearer on demand, a certain sum of money. It is therefore an interest-free promissory note payable on demand, which does not mean much since the government has, some years ago, taken the precaution to free itself from any obligation by establishing forced currency (Chapter 45, 3 George VI, of the Dominion statutes). Under that act, Bank of Canada notes are now legal tender for all, and in any private or public contract gold clauses or gold values are null and void.
I may add that since Canada's entry in the war and the appointment of a foreign exchange control board, the government even reserves the right to accept or refuse its own notes (that is to say its own pledges) in return for the American funds it holds. That is a security measure, but it nevertheless shows that the words "Pay to the bearer" have no longer any meaning.
A dominion bond is a promise on the part of the government to pay to the bearer, on demand, after the lapse of a certain period, that is on. such a date, such a sum. Like the bank note, the dominion bond is a promise to pay, but a promise that is deferred and bears interest. A promise to pay what? Merely interest-free notes issued by the Bank of Canada. After all, the only difference between a bank note and a dominion bond is that the Latter bears interest while the former does not. As the money so obtained from chartered banks and individuals is used by the government, the currency circulation in this country does not decrease, but neither does it increase. Such a situation obtains as long as individuals do not get rid of their bonds. If they do, the dam breaks; the government loses the benefit of the delay granted for the redemption of its bonds, and it fails to achieve one of the aims of the loan, which is to reduce temporarily or for the duration of the war the purchasing power of the people and to prevent them from spending.
It can thus be positively stated that while bearer-bonds issued to the public do not, in themselves, entail currency expansion to such a degree, they nevertheless open the way for it. This has been exemplified after the last war, in European countries where the people who held government bonds in France or those who in other countries held government

The Budget-Mr. LaCroix
bonds bearing interest at a low rate, started almost at the same time to put them on the market, within twelve months after the war, thereby causing a fantastic fall in the value of those bonds, a fall which also affected the currency of those countries. That is easy to understand) because while individuals cannot, in war time purchase anything or participate in the establishment of any industry and they are compelled to purchase government bonds, the reverse happens after the war, when they try to get rid of their government bonds as quickly as possible iri order to invest their money in industrial or business firms from which they can obtain a higher rate of interest. Although the war is not yet over, we can already notice such a trend. The figures published in connection with the second victory loan show that since their issue in February, 1942, no less than 339,000 bonds of $50 to $100 have been cashed by their original holders. In October last, they were coming back to Ottawa at the rate of 78,000 a month, or nearly 3,000 a day. Out of this total 339,000 bonds so cashed, 268,000 were fifty-dollar and
71,000	one hundred-dollar bonds. To date, they have been cashed at the chartered banks in a proportion of 24 per cent. As regards war savings certificates, they are being redeemed in a proportion of 34 per cent,, subscribers investing each month $6,000,000 in them and the government having to redeem them at the rate of $2,000,000 a month.
We have therefore every reason to wonder what will be done after the war by banks and insurance companies which at the present time pay no dividends on premiums. They will be looking for a rapid increase in their income by getting rid of their dominion bonds so as to improve their assets and obtain a 6 or 7 per cent return.
The same question may be asked about the chartered banks, because if they cannot at this time lend money to industrial or business firms and must be satisfied with a profit made up of the difference between what they pay to their depositors and what the government pays them for interest, we can ask ourselves whether they will not endeavour to lend money to industrial or business firms which will be reorganized after the war, in order to obtain a six per cent return, thus unloading upon the market, within twelve months after the end of hostilities, a supply of government bonds which will not be offset by a corresponding demand and which may cause a tremendous fall in the value of those bonds. The problem could easily be solved were all those bonds held by the Bank of Canada-that is to say, the government- 72537-99}
which would be careful in using them thereby ensuring the market stability that is essential if our currency is to remain sound.
The advantage of dealing solely with the Bank of Canada would eliminate from our budget that yearly $400,000,000 interest payment which we shall have to make to chartered banks or individuals; it would stabilize our currency and prevent the sudden appearance of inflation after victory has been achieved.
Besides, such a policy would lighten the tax burden on wage-earners, by this amount of $400 million subtracted from our budget.
I understand the policy followed by tf>e government so far has placed an increased amount of money in the hands of the public,, for the bank deposits from all sources, governmental, public and foreign, have soared from $3,144,000,000 in 1939, to $4,209,000,000 at the present time, an increase of over a billion dollars. This monetary expansion policy might have an extremely nefarious effect on the value of the Canadian dollar, if we allow the public and the chartered banks to keep too large an amount of government bonds. I sincerely believe that this practice of the dominion government of borrowing from the chartered banks is fraught with dangers; indeed, if, to-day, the chartered banks, in order to lend money, must not only use up their excess reserve of legal tender, but also find persons willing to go into debt, the situation will be reversed after the war, for a considerable number of people will then certainly be willing to borrow money from the banks in order ta engage in business ventures.	.
On the other hand, most of the industries' presently financed by dominion government funds and which, after the war, will own all developments paid for by the state, will endeavour to use their increased facilities by placing them on a peace-time footing. To attain this end they will no doubt throw on the market bonds and shares bearing a higher rate of interest than government bonds do at present and we shall then experience the strange situation of business enterprises fully financed by the government competing with the state in the financial field.
I sincerely regret that it has not been thought advisable to nationalize the banking system so as to make possible the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the war. I have no liking whatever for the chartered banks, especially in our province, where the-salary they pay or have paid their employees-is but a mere pittance. Moreover, the nationalization of these banks would not affect an institution which is indispensable in our province, the "caisses populaires" which are-
The Budget-Mr. LaCroix

authorized to do business with their members exclusively and are not allowed to extend loans beyond their actual capital. On the contrary, the nationalization of banking would he favourable to the expansion of "caisses populaires" which afford a more readily accessible paeans of accumulating savings, for .the deposits they would place with the Bank e>f Canada would be more secure; as it must not be forgotten that these institutions at the present time deposit their funds with the chartered banks. Besides, "caisses populaires" operate under a provincial statute entitled an act concerning cooperative syndicates (Chapter 290, Revised Statues of Quebec) and their loans are subject to prescription at the end of 30 years only, instead of 5 years.
Until now, the chartered banks have endeavoured to organize extremely powerful trusts, such as those formed when Mr. Holt became president of the Royal Bank. These trusts have caused economic disturbances heavily felt in the province of Quebec, especially in the fields of electric power and public utilities.
An hon. member has claimed, in this house, that we should oppose the nationalization of banks because some directors of the Bank of [DOT]Canada did not satisfy him. In answer, I should like to point out that no man is immortal, that any man may be replaced and that this does not in any way diminish the advantages nor does it alter the principle underlying the nationalization of our banking institutions.
I also wish, Mr. Speaker, to point out that the budget gives no consideration whatever to the fact that the upkeep of adolescents of convent or college age costs more to their parents than that of very young children. In their case, the least that should have been done was to allow for a greater proportion of the income tax to be refundable.
The budget submitted by the Minister of Finance does not afford sufficient protection to large families.
I also favour an increase in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, for the sums they now receive, if the cost of living is taken into account, is not even sufficient to cover the mere necessities of life.
I also regret that the control of our industries and businesses has been handed over to dollar a year men who, in most cases, are representatives of monopolistic industries and financial organizations already established in our midst and that, in the drafting of regulations for the control of the various industrial activities, they evidently follow the dictates of

the trusts, thereby contributing to the elimination of small industrial and business enterprises, especially in the province of Quebec. Indeed, it is hard to believe how many small concerns have been run out of business since these controllers, representing high finance, have taken charge of our national economy.
Those are the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why I shall vote for the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), which reads as follows:
That all the words after "That" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for the nationalization of the banking system so as to make possible the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the war;
And further this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for increases in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, or to make adequate provisions for veterans of the last or the present war, or their wives and dependents;
And further this house regrets the extent to which the government has vested the control of the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and finance."
However, I want to state that even if I support this amendment, to which I fully agree, it must not be construed that I adhere to all the theories expounded by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, for I feel that an hon. member of this house should consider it his duty to judge an amendment on its text, rather than on considerations as to what political group sponsors it.
In concluding, allow me to hope that, at least in connection with the problems of postwar reconstruction and reestablishment, the French Canadians will be represented on the committee organized under the chairmanship of Mr. Cyril James, principal of McGill university. Since Mr. Edouard Montpetit handed in his resignation, we have no representative on this committee. If the recommendations of the James committee are to be imbued with ideas' of sound ethnical duality, it is extremely important and urgent that a successor be appointed to Mr. Montpetit. This would give us an opportunity to make our influence felt in the drafting of post-war economic and social legislation. At present the James committee comprises seven English-speaking Canadians; it is therefore absolutely necessary that at least two Canadians of French extraction take part in future deliberations.
You will allow me, Mr. Speaker, to suggest to the government the names of two persons who rank among our best economists by virtue of their studies and achievements in the economic and social fields of our country; they

The Budget-Mr. Hansell
are Mr. Esdras Minville, of the Ecole des Hautes Etudes, of Montreal and Reverend Father Bouvier, a Jesuit. The works of these two men of striking personality on the matters that should arrest our attention in the postwar period are worthy of our best consideration.
A last suggestion and I am through. As Doctor James has but one secretary, Mr. J. E. MacKay, a French Canadian assistant should be appointed. Similarly, the executive committee on reconstruction has one secretary only. Mr. Robert Engranl. Why should we not give him a French-speaking assistant? Thus the French element of this country would be better able to take a larger part in parliamentary activities related to the organization of our post-war economy. Besides, it would thus be easier to give the members of parliament and the public reports written and published simultaneously in both official national languages.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day we were pleased to learn of the forthcoming visit of Mr. Anthony Eden to Canada. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made his statement to the house it will be recalled that I ventured to ask whether or not Mr. Eden could be called before the committee on post-war reconstruction and also before the committee on external affairs. The Prime Minister was quite gentlemanly in his answer and said that he would draw the request to the attention of Mr. Eden, but that of course Mr. Eden would be a very busy man. When I asked the question I thought I detected a bit of a murmur in some sections of this house, particularly that section directly opposite the Prime Minister; in fact one hon. member afterwards met me in the lobby and asked if it was my intention to have Mr. Eden subpoenaed. Well, of course he was not fooling me at all; I knew what was behind that remark. I am well aware that men of such distinction should be treated with the courtesy which their high diplomatic position deserves. I am not by any manner of means suggesting that Mr. Eden be subpoenaed before any committee, but I believe he has appeared before one or two very important congressional committees in the United States, as well as the senate committee on post-war reconstruction, and I maintain it is not unreasonable to expect that such a distinguished gentleman, holding such a particular and unique position in connection with world affairs and post-war design, should be called before the appropriate committees of this parliament whose responsibility it is to deal with these matters.
Some of us, Mr. Speaker, are particularly anxious in regard to what may be going on behind the scenes in respect of possible postwar problems. As soon as post-war problems are mentioned, someone is almost bound to rise and say, "Let us get on with the war." I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) is perhapsthe worst offender along this line; but let me tell him that if the particular kind of peace we are to have' is not settled, and settled right, before this war is over, he will be saying the same thing, "Let us get on with the war," some time about 1975, but it will be in respect of world war number three.
Post-war talks and conferences, to be of a permanent and effective nature, must deal with the problem of a new world order after the cessation of hostilities. The people themselves, therefore, have a right to know what sort of new world order is to be. The people have only one voice in these affairs, namely, the voice of their representatives in parliament. I am well aware of the fact that talks must be carried on by high diplomatic officials. I know that these negotiations must take place from time to time. I am not suggesting for one moment that all the details of these negotiations should be publicized north, soutli, east and west. But I do say that the representatives of the people assembling from time to time in parliament have a right to know what is going on behind the scenes.
I do not think I am the only one who deplores the fact that sometimes Canada seems to have to take the hindermost, that we seem to be on the tail end of everything. Certain conferences are held; diplomatic officials meet, and we wonder why Canada is not more distinctly represented. We wonder if certain things are being done, if certain things will be prepared and laid at the doorstep of the Canadian people for their acceptance, whether they like it or not. I say that is not just good enough for a nation like -Canada, in view of the magnificent effort she is now making in order to attain complete victory, and in a world which hopes to move on to a new order.
Mr. Eden arrived in America. No one seemed to know he was coming. Of course-it may not be best for the world to know, but the fact is that he arrived for these postwar talks. We wonder why our Prime Minister, who resides a flight of only an hour or two from Washington, could not be there, or send an appropriate representative. speechtext:
I am glad that that point is clear. Since it is clear, I promise you, sir, that when the committee does report I shall have something to say about it. There are certain individuals whom I would like to have called before the appropriate parliamentary committee. I should like to see Mr. Eden, not only meet here and speak to us on the floor of this house but meet with them. I would not object to that meeting being in
camera if necessary, but let Mr. Eden put his cards on the table and tell the post-war reconstruction committee just what is being done. Vice-President Wallace seems to be the spokesman in the United States for postwar planning, and I suggest that he or at least one of his representatives be called. The governor of the Bank of Canada and the deputy minister of finance should be called, A number of the big industrialists and perhaps the president of the bankers' association should also be called. These men could give valuable information in respect of what we may expect in the post-war world.
I should like to ask these men through the avenue of parliament a few pertinent questions. I should like to ask some of them why it is that they could not solve our pre-war depression. There is one thing that never happens in a discussion of these matters. They never try to discover the fundamental error of our present economic arrangements under which we are now living in comparative prosperity but under which, a few years ago, we went through one of the worst depressions the world has ever seen. They never try to discover that fundamental ill, and until that fundamental wrong is discovered, how on earth can we prescribe for the patient? It reminds me of the young doctor with very little experience who had a patient die on him. The doctor was very much surprised and said, "I do not understand why the man died. I gave him every sort of medicine I could think of." Of course, that was just the trouble. Similarly, the powers that prescribe this, that, and the other remedy without first discovering what the fundamental wrong is. I should like to ask those men who have been sitting in the saddle for so many years why it is that they could not cure the pre-war depression? I would ask them this very pertinent question: Why is it that they can find money enough to feed Hitler with bombs, but cannot find money enough to feed our aged parents with bread? If we need a battleship -it might cost five million dollars-five million dollars spring into existence. If the people cannot lend the money, the credit institutions of the country create it. It is simply a matter of mathematics.^ The whole monetary system is only a matter of figures; make no mistake about that. If we want a battleship, I say, a few million dollars at once spring into existence. If we want two battleships, then more million dollars spring into existence. If we want a dozen battleships-all right; there is the money. It does not matter where the battleships go. We hope, of course, that they will remain on top of the ocean and destroy
The Budget-Mr. Hansell

the fleets of the axis powers, but they may go to the bottom of the ocean. Still, the money is of no consequence. Yet somehow or another these supermen, with the superminds, cannot get a few extra dollars, not even the cost of living bonus, to give to our aged parents.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that there was nothing mysterious about the monetary system. It is simply that not until the last few years, when pressure has been exercised by groups, has the subject been brought out into the light of day. The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser), when he was speaking in the hotlse the other night, held up an Alberta prosperity certificate, and those who were in the chamber at the time know what happened. That prosperity certificate Was a dollar prosperity certificate. Oh, yes, this was "funny money," the hon. member said and went on, I will take a cent for it; I will take two cents. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) offered him two dollars. I have since asked the hon. member for Lethbridge if he was able to buy it, but he told me that he had not been able to buy it.

speechtext:
They did not have to go into debt to get it. Unless we recognize the fundamental wrong of the old order, we shall never be able to plan for the new. I am alarmed. I will use Mr. Churchill's phrase of last Sunday, "I will end my speech where I began." If I did not tell you, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Churchill said that, you might think I was attempting to he funny. But I will close where I started. Surely we are looking forward to a new world. When it will come I do not know; I trust it will come soon. But if we are to have a world in which there is any security we must plan now; we must know where we are going; we must find out what is fundamentally wrong and correct those fundamental errors. If we fail here, we shall fail those who are sacrificing so much; we shall fail them as we failed those who gave their blood on the battlefields of world war number one. Let us not permit these things to happen behind the scenes and find ourselves saddled with a system which eventually will take us into a slavery even worse than that of the dark ages.
In conclusion, I would say a word with respect to the amendment upon which, perhaps, we shall soon vote. I refer to the subamendment moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group. I am dis-

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
appointed with the wording of this subamendment. I believe that our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends, while wording it as they did, could have added to our amendment instead of deleting it. They call for the nationalization of the chartered banks. Personally it does not matter to me a particle whether the chartered banks are nationalized or not. I could vote for this subamendment and be happy about it; and perhaps I will; I may so decide during the last second or two; but I know that if I do, I am placed in the position of voting to strike out our amendment. I say in all kindness to my hon. friends that amendments of that kind do not tend to draw these two progressive groups any closer together. I think we should be able to come to an understanding with regard to some of these matters.
May I, in conclusion, place on the record a brief statement with respect to the nationalization of banks? It is an extract from a speech by Major C. H. Douglas at Oslo, Norway, in 1935:
The institution and keeping of the national credit account does not require any nationalization of the banks. As a matter of fact, such nationalization would be a great mistake. I am not myself, for instance, an advocate of the nationalization of banks. I believe this again to be one of those misapprehensions so common in regard to these matters, for the nationalization of banks is merely an administrative change: it does not mean a change in policy, and a mere administrative change cannot be expected to produce any result whatever in regard to this matter. A change in monetary policy can be made without interfering with the administration or ownership of a single bank in the world.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are agitated because my time is gone. Thank you very much for your indulgence: and once more I promise the post-war reconstruction committee that I will talk a little about them when they bring down their next report.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This budget debate has been like a long, cold, hard winter; many of us have wondered when it was going to be over. No doubt the last speeches are like the April blizzards which we occasionally get. But I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that mine will be short-the thaw will soon come.
About this time in a budget debate there is a sort of open season on banks. I, too, have unpleasant memories of my banker. I frequently have distressing experiences; my bank manager calls me and says unkind things to me, using a lot of long words which I do not rightly understand. Therefore if there is to be an open season on banks, I should like to be 72537-100
armed with the tommy gun of my hon. friends on the left and let loose, because I could have a great deal of fun.
But before we do that, let us see what we are to do if we should nationalize the banks. Let us see what these much abused chartered banks have done for us.
I do not pretend to be an expert on money. But I think I understand a little about what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said in his budget speech. In 1942 the new financing in Canada amounted to the colossal sum of $4,290,000,000, of which the two war loans came to approximately $1,978,000,000, leaving $2,312,000,000 in short-term government money, which was financed very largely by the chartered banks. There was a certain amount of municipal financing, but it was small compared with what was obtained by the government from the chartered banks.
All of us know about the income tax. For the coming year the income tax is expected to raise $568,000,000; the corporation tax, $805,000,000, and the excise tax, $477,000,000, or a total of $1,850,000,000 as against the 1941 total of $1,261,000,000.
Let us look at what the banks did. The government admitted that it borrowed from the chartered banks $790,000,000, and from the Bank of Canada $443,000,000, or a total of $1,233,000,000, almost as great a sum as was raised by all the principal methods of direct taxation. There, it seems to me, we have an asset capable of producing these sums of money in this very distressing financial year. Therefore, before we do anything with the banks I should like to have explained to me, and I think the majority of simple-minded persons like myself would be glad of that explanation, what we are to put in their place that can lend this money or can fulfil the functions that the banks have fulfilled during this year. We should know these things before we start nationalizing or socializing the chartered banks. I do not know where we should have been without the chartered banks this last year.
As to the war loans, in the fiscal year 1942 there were two war loans totalling nearly $2 billion. I should like to know what happened to those bonds. It was currently said in Toronto and other financial centres that people bought the bonds, kept them for a short time and then sold them back on the market. In fact it is commonly said that the big corporations bought millions of dollars worth of bonds, held them for a few weeks and then turned them back on the market, which presumably had to be supported by the government. Who bough*

The Budget-Mr. Adamson

those bonds from the big interests, and where are they now? Were they taken by the chartered banks; were they taken by the finance department, or what happened to them? I know many instances of people buying bonds, holding them a short time and then turning them back on the market. Who supported that market? The government has supported the market. But was it not helped by the chartered banks, and were not individual subscribers helped by the chartered banks? If we start to destroy these institutions, who is going to fulfil that function?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The national bank.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think so. The national bank is the government.
I notice that private bond issues are beginning to come out again. I see that the Imperial Tobacco companj' has put out a bond issue of $10 million ten-year bonds, and the credit of the company is so good that they pay only one-quarter of one per cent more than the government pays. They issued these ten-year bonds at three and a quarter per cent, and bonds for a somewhat longer term bear three and three-eighths per cent. But it seems to me that in war time every dollar raised from the people should go to support the war. I know that in England private financing was virtually prohibited, except for very special purposes, for the entire duration of the war.
These Imperial Tobacco company bonds have already been sold. What did the company Want that money for? Surely tobacco is not a war necessity. But they got the money, got it very easily; the bonds were sold before the advertisement appeared, showing the excellent credit of the company and showing how much money there must be in the country.
The Minister of Finance did not like having to borrow the amount of money that he borrowed from the banks on short-term notes at one half and three-quarters of one per cent; I think three-quarters of one per cent was the most he paid. I notice that some treasury notes were sold to-day at one-half of one per cent. It seems to me that without those financial institutions that are capable of lending the government this money, the government would find itself in greater difficulty than it does now. I do not profess to be a financier or to know a great deal about banking, but to my mind that is a problem which has to be explained before we can entertain any idea of nationalization of those institutions.

There is one small matter I wish to take up with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson). It concerns propaganda. As a member of this house I receive a great deal of propaganda; we all do. We receive propaganda from many countries. I even received some from Germany-not recently. I received it from the Free French, from Chile, and from many other countries. The other day I asked the British minister of information in New York to send me some pamphlets to distribute. The invoice came to me marked "No commercial value, property of the British government, not salable." But when I tried to clear it through the customs the customs put an arbitrary value of $15 on it and charged me 30 per cent duty. The impression that gave me was that it is an effort on the part of the government to stop British propaganda. Every other type of propaganda comes in free, but British propaganda is charged 30 per cent. I think we should have some explanation of that.
We had a debate in this house concerning the aluminum corporation, taking a great part of one afternoon. I should like to mention the production of the four other main nonferrous metals, and to show what has been done in their production in Canada by private enterprise. These four main non-ferrous metals are lead, zinc, copper and nickel. In 1942 our production of non-ferrous metals was 1,100,000 tons, which proportionately was four times as great as the production of the United States. The additional aluminum production probably represents a great increase even over that. This was all done by four or five of the largest mining corporations in the world; I need not name them. It may be said that no doubt these corporations made colossal profits on the sale of these non-ferrous metals. Well, at the beginning of the war an agreement was made with the British government under which the prices of copper, zinc and lead were stabilized at a level a great deal lower than the then market price. Let us look at the prices these great corporations are now getting for their metals. To-day copper is being sold to Great Britain at 25 per cent less than the domestic United States price, zinc at one-third of the United States price and lead at one-half that price. In my opinion it was a very patriotic and thoroughly fine gesture on the part of these great corporations to obligate themselves to sell these metals at these prices from the beginning of the war.
Let us look now at what happened in the United States and elsewhere in regard to other necessary metals such as chromite, manganese, tungsten and mercury, all essential metals practically not produced at all in Canada.

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
They are selling at two and a half times the pre-war price. Consequently I think these large mining corporations in Canada, in selling non-ferrous metals at from one-half to one-third the former price, have demonstrated a commendable and praiseworthy attitude.
In connection with these metals, for yearn we have been greatly worried in regard to the wastage or what one might call the high-grading of our major metal deposits, because there has been no major discovery of base metals in the last ten or fifteen years. Perhaps the last major deposit of base metal in Canada was made at Noranda some fifteen or seventeen years ago. Well, Mr. Speaker, you cannot expect a mining industry to continue unless new discoveries are made. The point I wish to make to-night is that we have seen how vital these metals are both in peace and in war, and yet no major discoveries have been made, certainly for the last ten years. Why is that? I think the reason is that the taxation policy of the government has not encouraged prospecting parties to go out looking for discoveries in order to develop the country. The policy has been to penalize in every way anyone who showed the pioneer spirit. Mind you, _ to-day it takes millions to bring in a mine; it is not small business any more. If an individual goes out and discovers a property, at every step from the raw prospect right up to the producing mine the government tax-gatherer sits in and taxes every move. You cannot treat mines like that; you cannot tax a mine until it is making a profit, that is if you wish to have a healthy mining industry. The first sign we have had in this country that this principle has been realized is in the present budget, but it should have been put into effect years ago.
The mines belong to the people who discover and develop them, but people who discover and develop mines have a great responsibility to the state, quite apart from seeing that the mine is properly run, that labour is properly looked after, that the mine is kept safe, and so on. They have a responsibility to develop the country, and I believe our taxation should be so arranged that mines now in production may be encouraged to continue in order that the country may be developed. Otherwise we will find ourselves with a steadily diminishing production of metals, and there is nothing so vital to us in Canada as a large production of metals. In this connection we are probably changing over from the production of lead, zinc and copper metallurgy to the production of lighter metals such as aluminum and magnesium ; and if there are deposits of magnesium the government should give every encouragement to their development.
The other evening I was interested to hear the principal of Queen's university say that he hoped we would return to a gold standard. I thought perhaps the roof would fall off; it did not, but sometime it may. But I thoroughly agree with that gentleman. There must be a metallic coverage; our paper currency has never been satisfactory for long terms and for international trade without a metallic coverage or conversion for our famous dollar bills that go into and out of the banker's window. What will be the price of gold or how it will be arranged no one can tell at this moment, but I think it goes without saying that we shall have to get back to some form of gold as a monetary standard. I hear criticism of this suggestion. Well, we shall be able to do witlr-out the gold standard the day my hon. friends and I are in a poker game, my hon. friend holding a full house of aces up on kings, and I with a busted straight. I lay my cards face down, and say I have four aces, and the pot is mine. The day he pushes the money over to me, without expecting me to turn my cards face up, that day we shall not need the gold standard. But until we get international goodwill and international trust to such a high degree, we must have some means of international currency. Human nature is like that.
With reference to the pioneer spirit I should like to refer briefly to the Steep Rock situation. Here we have a development which has been known about for a number of years, one of the greatest iron ore deposits ever discovered on this continent in the last fifty years. Certainly it is the greatest discovery since that of the Mesaba iron range. It is extremely rich, and an extremely valuable deposit of ore. But on account of lack of the pioneer spirit, where did we have to go to have the development financed? We had to go to Washington. Not only did we have to go to Washington, but we had to go to the reconstruction finance corporation, an organization of the United States government. That organization lent $5,000,000 at four per cent, and another $2,025,000 was lent by Otis and Company of Cleveland at 5i per cent. So long as the development is financed, and it goes into production, it makes no difference to me. But why could we not have done the financing in Canada? Are we-so pigeon-hearted about this magnificent deposit that there was nobody in Canada who would risk a sum as small as $5,000,000 to develop that iron ore deposit? I am sure $10,000,000 could easily be raised by a tobacco company. But when it comes to the development of one of our greatest resources, we cannot raise the money, and we have to go. to the United States government.
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

The facts about Steep Rock are well known. They were in, the press and in the trade papers. I mention them here for only one purpose and with one idea, namely, to show the opportunities we as Canadians are passing up every day in the week, simply because we are not awake to the possibilities in our own country. We are not alive to developments. We have lost the pioneering spirit. The men who pioneered in the oldi days did not permit their work to be lessened by the whims of government, or by budgets. They took chances on their country, and developed it. Those men are not in the field to-day, and the country is suffering. They are not there because this and previous governments have not encouraged the pioneer spirit. Men have been almost forced to put their money in the safety of savings accounts and life insurance policies, so that it could be safe from taxation. What we must do, add do almost immediately, is to see to it that this country is developed by the courageous foresight of individuals. When they do have success let us show that we are * proud of them, instead of treating them almost as criminals.

Before the vote is taken on the two amendments I believe I should say a word or two, inasmuch as the question at issue is largely between the two so-called progressive, smaller groups in the house, namely, the Social Credit and Cooperative Commonwealth Federation groups. On March 9, I moved this amendment to the budget, as it appears at page 1092 of Hansard:
This house regrets that the government still disregards the possible uses of government-created national money to the end that in so far as taxation and the borrowing of the people's savings fail to meet government expenditures the government might employ national money:
(a)	To relieve the debt situation which threatens the ownership and control of a great many private businesses, factories, farms and other means of production.
(b)	To pay farmers and other primary producers fair prices thereby stimulating the production of food.
(c)	To provide workers with adequate purchasing power.
(d)	To alleviate the distress of the aged and others in needy circumstances.

(e)	To prevent inflation by the subsidizing of industry where costs are uncontrollable, adopting where necessary a more aggressive and consistent rationing policy.
On the same day the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) moved a subamendemnt in which he proposed to strike out completely the amendment of the Social Credit group. I wish to spend a few minutes on the significance of the fact that the Social Credit amendment was to be struck out completely. It will be noticed that there was to be no addition to it, but that it was to be struck out, the implication apparently being that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are opposed not only to all the objects the Social Credit group proposed to attain, but also to the method by which this group proposed to attain them.
