speechtext: There is no suggested method in the amendment.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If that be the case, then quite clearly these two groups are diametrically opposed. There may, however, be some means of arriving at cooperation by the two groups. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" in the amendment be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for the nationalization of the banking system so as to make possible the full utilization of the Bank of Canada for the financing of the war;
and further this house regrets the failure of the government to provide for increases in the amounts paid to old age and blind pensioners, or to make adequate provisions for veterans of the last or the present war, or their widows and dependents;
and further this house regrets the extent to which the government has vested the control of the Canadian economy in monopolistic industry and finance."
In the first place, I desire to point out that all the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation need to do is to add about five or six more paragraphs to this amendment and they will have covered the whole gospel from Genesis to Revelations. Then, if anyone voted against their amendment he could be accused of voting against some good thing, no matter what good thing was being considered. I maintain that an amendment of that sort, whether or not it is designed to accomplish the end, results in confusing the issue. What I believe is essential at the present time is to keep the issue clear. All we need to do is to listen to the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Adamson) who has just resumed his seat and those of

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) uttered in the chamber this very day to see how widely the opinions of people in this dominion can differ. Surely we ought to try to keep the issue clear.
As far as the Social Credit group is concerned, the issue is simply this: Is there any means whereby the state can obtain money other than by taxation or by incurring debt? If there is, then there is some hope for the nation; if there is not, then there is apparently no hope for Canada anywhere. The Social Credit movement has aimed constantly ever since coming to this house to keep before the house this one issue: Is there any source of money without taxation and without debt?
The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has proposed the nationalization of the banking system. What do they believe they can achieve by nationalizing the banking system? Do they believe that money can be obtained from a nationalized banking system without capital debt and without interest? If they believe that, then the only difference between the Social Credit and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation groups on that particular point is whether or not you can derive this debt-free money, this money freed from capital debt and interest more successfully from a national bank, or from an individually owned bank, or from no bank at all. Social Credit contends that the state does not necessarily have to have a bank in order to issue national money, any more than the Dominion of Canada had to have a bank in order to issue the S26,000,000 to which I have previously referred and which was issued during the last war. They used that money to help finance their war expenditures between 1914 and 1917, and no bank was used. The treasury board issued the money under the Finance Act of 1914, and that money was free of debt and free of interest. The question is whether the principle established by the issuing of that money is a sound principle which could be used to-day to greatly relieve the distress which we are now suffering in conducting the war and to minimize the dangers which we shall have to face at the conclusion of the war and which were forecast so well by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard.
If it is possible to create money without the use of a bank, then why bother about nationalizing the banks? That is the natural question the Social Credit group would ask. If you nationalize the banks, are you not in danger of complicating the situation for years? That is the consideration which should be in our minds. The passage from Major C. H. Douglas
which was read by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) earlier in the evening indicates quite clearly the attitude of that great leader upon that question. Major C. H. Douglas is the originator of the Social Credit movement; he is the teacher, and his opinion respecting the ownership of banks and what effect it would have upon financing the national concern is of importance.
What has been the effect of nationalizing the banks in days gone by? Let us refer to our own Bank of Canada. When it was proposed that we should have a Bank of Canada, government owned, I am sure the general opinion throughout the west was that Canada would be able to draw money from that bank to finance her going concern. I am sure it never dawned on the people of the west that after the government of Canada had a central bank we would have to borrow from that bank just as though it were the Bank of England or some other private owner of money and then pay back the money borrowed and with interest. That concept would be a most astounding one to any person in the west who looked upon the national ownership of banks as a desirable thing.
If the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believe that by nationalizing the banks we shall be able to get money free from debt and free from interest; if they are completely convinced that it is necessary to nationalize the banks, then probably we should grant them a certain amount of consideration. Personally I do not believe that that is necessary. I feel we have gone as far in nationalizing the banks-as is necessary when we have nationalized the Bank of Canada. I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard who said this afternoon that the chartered banks should remain in private hands and should be used as a part of the productive system of the country. It is a fundamental stand of the Social Credit movement that the productive system of the country in every respect should be in private hands, that by maintaining it in private hands the greatest degree of motivation will be obtained. We favour the individual ownership of the means of production. If the chartered banks, which loan money for commercial purposes, are to be looked upon as part of the productive system, then in order to be logical we must have the commercial banks in private hands.

speechtext:
When the hon. member says that he believes in individual ownership,, does he exclude corporate ownership, or does he believe in corporations and trusts as well as in individual ownership?
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A corporation is just what the name implies. The word "corporation" comes from the Latin "corpus", which means body. The body acts as an individual; consequently a corporation is an individual in the eyes of the law. It is embodied in one body. The trust or the monopoly is an abuse of individual ownership. It is something that has gone too far, and the fact that it exists is evidence that there has been mismanagement or that there is weakness in the system under which it has developed. The Social Credit attitude is that you would not destroy the corporation; you would simply rearrange the set of rules under which it acts in order to prevent abuses from developing.
We feel that the question of motivation is all important. Let us remember that if we change the system under which we are working to-day, we change it perhaps for a hundred years; we change it for our children and our grandchildren to grow up under. Therefore we want to build a system which will motivate to the highest possible degree activities of the finest kind. We want the people to get out and work and develop themselves while they produce. While they produce we want them also to have a higher degree of the abundance of life. We as a Social Credit group believe that we can [DOT]obtain these objects through individual ownership better than by state or social ownership. We are granting at the same time, judging from anything which has been said by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation since I have been in this house, that they do not indicate very clearly just what is meant by social ownership or social control. As I said the other day, the stand of the party seems to be a bit shifty on this matter, and it is very difficult to tell just what is meant by social ownership. For example, they do not favour, if I understand them aright, having farms all taken over and controlled socially. They favour individual ownership to that degree. I am wondering if they favour taking over the small town stores and managing them socially. I imagine not.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly not.

I have had my eyes open and I shall show that they have been opened much wider than the hon. member's have been, judging by some of the things he has said on the floor of this house very recently.
Between these two amendments, Mr. Speaker, it is the desire of the Social Credit movement to keep the issue clear. I do not believe that my hon. friend and his party favour allowing great concerns with power to dictate to the government with respect to the economic affairs of this country. We Social Crediters would not agree to allowing great concerns to run at large with unrestricted competition any mure than would the members of the Liberal party or of the Progressive Conservative party. I do not suppose you could find one-tenth of the members of this house who would be in favour of unrestricted competition, unrestricted development of monopolies and trusts. Every one would favour some regulation of them, just as the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) indicated the other day. I am not sure that I would go as far as he was prepared to go, but perhaps that was because I was not absolutely clear as to what he meant by the words he used. So much depends upon the words you use and what you mean by them. There are words of large connotation and words of very indefinite connotation, the use of which tends to confuse an issue.
As I said a moment ago, we want to keep the issue clear. In this vote which we are going to take on the two amendments we Social Crediters shall endeavour to keep the issue clear. We do not propose to be mixed up with any question of old age pensions or anything of that sort. We realize fully that if we vote against the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment, immediately their propaganda machine will spread all over the dominion that this group voted against old age pensions.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

speechtext: No, no.

speechtext:
We are glad to have that assurance, but our past experience makes us suspicious.
1 wish to refer now to some false conceptions of the Social Credit stand which have been manifest in the addresses of some hon. members in this debate, false conceptions which it is impossible for me to comprehend.
I turn first of all to the words of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who according to his own words has been very, very careful to observe just what has been said and draw his own conclusions. At page 1106 of Hansard he said :
We cannot regard money as anything but a rough and ready measure and medium of circulation for goods. It seems to me that my hon. friends to my left mistake money for wealth. In other words, they mistake the < shadow for the substance. In my view sound money is money that is related to goods and services.
May I just make a comment here, Mr. Speaker. I have not the time to review all the speeches which I have delivered in this house, but in the first speech I delivered in 1936, to which any hon. member may refer if he desires to check up what I say, I specifically pointed out that in a certain year in United States economic history the people of the United States produced $60,000,000,000 worth of goods, yet all the money which was distributed in the United States with which those goods might have been bought amounted to only $45 billion, and of that $45 billion $5 billion were put away in life insurance and in other kinds of savings, leaving a net of only $40 billion with which to buy $60 billion worth of goods. That indicated that there was a scarcity of purchasing power in the hands of the people of the United States in that particular year, and the shortage of purchasing power had to be made up. I argued that the way in which that could be made up was by monetizing the $20 billion worth of goods and distributing that money in the hands of the people, thereby enabling them to buy the $20 billion worth of goods, or the goods from abroad for which they might exchange those goods. If that was not clear and unmistakable I do not know how illustrations and words could make a matter clear. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was here when I made that speech and he has been here when I have made every other speech since, or at all events Hansard has been available if he really wanted to know what Social Credit's attitude was on money as related to goods. So that it has been certainly easy for him to find out.
May I refer to one further speech I made. On March 8, 1938, I moved a vote of want of confidence in the government and delivered a speech which lasted something like two hours. My object was to make unequivocally clear just this very point which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar professes to be in doubt about. I laid down there this fundamental principle, that the amount of money which a country can have depends upon the goods-and-services-producing-and-consuming power of the country.
Let me say one more thing. I have never yet referred to a booklet which I took the trouble to write just for the sake of men like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar who could not gather the meaning of what I had to say from my speeches in the house. It is called "Money the Master Key."

If my hon. friend
has read it, he will find that time and time again reference is made in it to that very point, the statement being repeated that the amount of money which a community can have depends upon the goods-and-services-producing-power of the community. So there should be no doubt at all regarding that matter.
Now I quote a passage from Major Douglas to indicate his stand. These are his words:
It must be obvious that the real limit of the rate at which something representing purchasing power could be issued to the public is equal to the maximum rate at which goods can be produced.
I hope that disposes of that matter.
Now I turn to the words of the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross). The hon. member in his speech, as recorded at page 1329 of Hansard of March 17, made this remark: My hon. friends of the Social Credit group would wreck the whole thing by issuing worthless paper money.
The hon. member for Macleod very properly called out, "It is a tie." The hon. member for Moose Jaw had no vestige of excuse for making any such absurd remark as that after having sat here in the presence of social creddters and having conversed in private with social crediters so that he could obtain a correct conception of their views. As long as members persist in misconceptions of this kind deliberately held, apparently, I fail utterly to see how we are going to get anywhere at all in this country.
May I refer now to what the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) said the other evening. He made this remark:
I will not attempt to speak on monetary reform, for the good and simple reason that I do not understand it.
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

He made it quite clear that he did not understand it. He didl not need to tell us that, because he illustrated it clearly. He proceeded to say:
I think, however, I understand enough to know that the monetary reform offered by our friends from Alberta is neither sound nor sensible, that is as they expound it here and as they are supposed to expound it in the press, although frankly I do not hold them responsible for all that is said about them in the press.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley is ordinarily a careful man, and I have gathered from what he has said in the past that he is endeavouring to get things straight. The amazing thing is why, if he was not able to gather from what social crediters said in the House of Commons the truth about their theory, he did not come and ask one of us to explain it to him or study a book from which he could learn this important theory.
He indicated that it is very hard to tell what social crediters believe from what is said in the House of Commons.' I ask the hon. member what chance he would have of learning what Liberals believe from what they state in the House of Commons, or how he would get an accurate conception of what Conservatives believe by hearing what they say in the house. What chance has any hon. member of expounding here in any kind of satisfying detail the whole philosophy and technique of the beliefs that he maintains?
I contend that the solution of our troubles lies in money, in the ability of the state to obtain money which can be spent into circulation rather than lent into circulation, and can be acquired by the state without increasing debt and without increasing interest charges.
Just before I leave this question of the two amendments, may I point out that the Social Credit group, in order to clarify the issue, and to prevent any possibility of misrepresentation in this country concerning their stand, intend to refrain from holding sternly to their attitude on the banking system, and will vote for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment. We shall have an interesting time seeing what the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation will do with respect to the Social Credit amendment.
I should like to refer to just one or two other things which are involved in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation amendment. I think we can accept all they say about old age pensions, and all they say regarding giving veterans more pay. Surely everyone in the house agrees with these things; certainly we do. As to what they say about too great 
monopolistic industrial and financial control, we all agree with that. So that we can accept quite easily those parts of their amendment.
I should like to show some hon. members, who have had so much to say in derision of monetary proposals for the solution of our difficulty, just how foolish they are, or at least how much out of step they are with some of the very best thinking in the world to-day. In order to do so, I will refer again to little pamphlets which have been mentioned several times in this house, in particular the report of the London chamber of commerce issued on May 12, 1942. I read from the first page the following statement:
The chamber submits that constantly raised tariffs, the imposition of quotas and prohibitions, and other signs of growing economic belligerency between the nations in the inter-war * period, were not the result of stupidity nor ill-will but were, on the contrary, imposed for most compelling reasons. They represented attempts by the nations to defend themselves against very real and pressing dangers. The chamber is convinced that until those dangers are recognized and removed, a direct attack upon trade barriers can serve no useful purpose but will, on the contrary, merely increase fear. In short, trade barriers are not themselves the disease but merely the symptoms of the disease.
The important question is, what is the disease? What is the cause of it? May I read another excerpt?
It was palpably absurd that nations should be desperately anxious to export more of their real wealth to other nations than they received in return. It was equally absurd that men in want of the necessaries of life should be denied the money with which to buy them because there was a superabundance of those necessaries and therefore their services were not required to make more.
With that, I believe,, all hon. members will agree. I read from page 4:
The limiting factor in the production of real wealth has, however, been the failure to distribute to would-be consumers enough money to buy the potential output, and goods are not for long produced if there are no buyers.
That is an extremely important point. May I read another:
The system of distributing purchasing power was evolved during an age of scarcity, i.e., an age in which there were not enough goods to go round. This system aimed, therefore, at ensuring maximum production with minimum consumption.
A few moments ago hon. members heard the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) raise the question, why do we not examine the present financial system with the object of discovering wherein lies the flaw; and then, why do we not concentrate our attention on the removal of that flaw? May I

The Budget-Mr. Blcickmore
read from page 5, because the people who drafted this report have done the veiy thing which the hon. member for Macleod suggested:
... it was clearly necessary to increase the purchasing power of the masses in order to provide buyers, without which the goods would not, for long, be produced.
From page 7, I select the following:
The chamber cannot therefore support any scheme which, in the economic sphere, relies upon some supranational authority (which in practice must mean the most powerful nation ir nations) to dictate to the weaker nations yhat their internal economic policy shall be.
On page 8:
It believes, on the contrary, that the largest measure of cooperation between nations will be realized when fear of financial and economic domination from outside is removed, and each nation is entirely free to cooperate or not as it wishes; the extent of that cooperation also being within its own control.
May I stop here to observe that to social erediters that is an extremely important point. As hon. members will have noticed, during this year we have continually urged that every care be adopted in Canada to prevent this country from being entangled in some international organization which will limit her power to manage her own affairs.
Under the system which we propose, the dominion can keep control of her affairs independent of every nation on the face of the earth, except in so far as she must exchange some of her goods for goods which she cannot produce; and the number of goods which she must bring in from outside is surprisingly small. The result is that Canada is admirably endowed for becoming an economically self-sufficient unit, and what we maintain is that Canada should become a self-sufficient unit economically. She will never do that by entangling herself in any supranational organization: she will do that by distributing purchasing power within her own bounds.
May I now read further from page 9 of this report:
What is necessary is to improve the technique for the internal provision of money, so as to convert this human demand into effective demand.
If the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation knows how to do that better than the Social Credit people do, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation proposals are undoubtedly the best proposals for the Dominion of Canada at the present time. Otherwise Social Credit is the best. I read again on:
These surplus exports might confer a benefit on some countries if they were sent as a gift; and the recipient country had an internal
financial mechanism capable of distributing enough purchasing power to its people to enable them to buy excess imports of consumers' goods in addition to, instead of in competition with, the goods already there.
Again:
The chamber submits that international trade must now be raised to its true function, that is, nothing more nor less than an exchange of goods and services of a mutually advantageous character.
A quotation from page 10:
Instead of trying to equate supply with effective demand, the chamber advocates that, in future, effective demand should be equated with supply.
Hon. members will recognize that this amounts simply to the creation of purchasing power within the country and the distribution of that purchasing power to enable the people to buy the goods which they are able to produce, or to buy the goods which they are able to trade their surplus for, which is exactly the contention that the social erediters have made before this house ever since 1936. The report states, as one of the problems which a satisfactory system must be designed to solve:
The distribution internally of the purchasing power necessary to enable the nations to consume the whole of their own production: if this were done they could equally consume the goods of other nations which they might exchange for their own production.
And again on page 11:
The chamber, having considered whether there is any system which would achieve, wholly or partially, the solution of all the above problems, generally accepts the principles laid down in "A Twentieth Century Economic System" especially in respect of blocked credits for the payment of international obligations.
May I now read four short excerpts from this same "A Twentieth Century Economic System". This is from page 15:
How to distribute purchasing power to the mass of the people is therefore the most pressing and urgent internal problem of every advanced nation.
On page 17:
No excuse is made for having considered at some length under-consumption, which is synonomous with unemployment, since it is submitted that this is a root problem which must be solved, unless all hope of the survival of our civilization is to be abandoned.

Mr. Speaker, the statement I wish to make is rather short and it could be made as a question of privilege. Yesterday I sent you a copy of this, but in view of the strong desire of all hon. members to conclude this debate immediately, if the house will allow me to make that statement to-morrow as a question of privilege I shall be glad to postpone it until that time.

I cannot give any ruling on a question of privilege unless I know what it is. If the hon. member wishes to raise this question of privilege to-morrow, he will have to put that question according to the rules of the house. I cannot make any promise as to how I shall view a question of privilege made by the hon. member.

I wished also to make a few remarks on the budget in connection with the rationing of sugar and butter which I contend is causing some injustice to certain classes of people, but in view of the fact that everyone seems to be in a hurry I will postpone these observations until later. Following my declaration in the house that since the beginning of the war the protection accorded the St. Lawrence has not been adequate, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) made a statement on March 17, as reported at page 1345 of Hansard. He said:
I say my friend would have pursued a more loyal course to his own constituents and to this country if he had investigated these rumours and endeavoured to allay the fears of his people.
The minister's allegations found an echo in some of the newspapers, especially in the Ottawa Journal of March 19 which published an editorial which was altogether wrong. The minister's statement which I have just quoted was at the conclusion of a narration of facts which he made as an answer to a speech I delivered in the house on March 15. I consider it a duty toward myself as well as toward my constituents to show that if one takes into consideration the minister's allegations in regard to those I made myself, he must come to the conclusion that before making such an accusation the minister should have ascertained that he had succeeded in denying all my contentions or at least the most important ones. One of the important charges I made is contained in a statement to be found at page 1269 of Hansard. This statement is:
The people down there know that our planes have never participated in any battle in the course of which ships have been sunk by enemy submarines.

The Budget-Mr. Roy
I cannot find any answer to that statement in the minister's speech. The only reference is to be found at page 1342 of Hansard, where he is reported as saying:
But I have it from the air staff that their aircraft have carried out eight attacks on submarines in the St. Lawrence area, during each of which depth charges were dropped.
As everyone can see, that is neither an answ'er nor a denial.
Another important declaration which I made is found at page 1269 of Hansard. I quote:
On September 15 one submarine was seen only one mile from the lighthouse at Cap des Rosiers, at exactly eleven o'clock in the morning. The keeper of the lighthouse, Mr. Joseph Ferguson, telephoned right away to Captain Cote, who is in charge of what we call the A.D.C., and also in charge of the telephone exchange at Cap des Rosiers. He is also manager of the telephone exchange at that point. The same Mr. Ferguson telephoned to Fox River, to another man of the A.D.C., Mr. Walter Lequesne. He said he had seen a submarine exactly one mile northeast of the lighthouse, and had placed a board to indicate the right spot where he had noticed the submarine. That was exactly eleven o'clock in the morning. A few minutes later from the lighthouse a convoy could be seen coming up from the southeast, toward that very spot. It was evident that something was going to happen to the convoy when it would reach there. There is about ten miles as the bird would fly from Fox River to the place where the submarine had been seen and where two boats were sunk a few minutes later.
The young ladies of Mr. Walter Lequesne, through the call from Mr. Walter Ferguson of Cap des Rosiers, had been informed of the fact that the convoy was coming up, and that the submarine was there. These young ladies, and the young ladies of Mr. Albert Morris of Fox River, climbed up inside the church steeple to watch what was going to happen down there. A few minutes later the convoy was coming up, right on top of the submarine. The torpedoes started to run on the waves, and two ships went down. The first one was struck at 12.21 p.m. and the second one at 12.22 p.m. The first one went down at 12.28 p.m. and the second at 12.32 p.m. No aeroplane showed around there to help the corvettes.
I went on to explain that the people of Fox River were watching to see what would happen. Again I quote from Hansard, at page 1269:
There were some corvettes and destroyers in the convoy. But why is it that the naval officers of the Gaspe base and all the men who could have taken care of the situation, and who are supposed to have the necessary powers to act by themselves, without being obliged to call for orders from Halifax or Quebec, did not give the proper orders to change the course of that convoy? They had plenty of time to do it. The civilian population knew what was about to happen. They were watching the events. It was only the navy and the air force which did not seem to be aware of those facts. There surely was a lack of organization.
Surely there was a lack of organization, and the minister, in dealing with this statement of
mine, could not deny it. In fact he tried to give some sort of explanation which is rather a confirmation. We find the minister's explanation at page 1343 of Hansard, where he said:
In this case on September 15 the naval officer at Quebec did not receive any word about the submarine until after the submarine had launched its torpedoes. I do not know whose fault that was, if it was anybody's fault. I can understand that on a long stretch of coast where people may have to go some little distance to a telephone and make a call to someone else, who in turn perhaps has to relay the communication to some other person, some time might be lost. But I do know the time at which the naval officer at Quebec received the information, and unfortunately it was then too late to do anything about the matter. Submarines strike very quickly and they can submerge very quickly.
I do not know definitely. I assume there would be a telephone in the lighthouse, but I do not know how far the man who saw the submarine had to go to reach the lighthouse; I do not know how long it took him to get there, nor do I know how long it took to get the call through to Quebec. All I am telling this house is that the naval officer at Quebec did not get the information until it was too late to do anything about it.
I shall now mention another statement which I made on that occasion, a statement which has been improperly represented by the minister of naval affairs, and which has brought forth an editorial in the Ottawa Journal which I shall presently quote. The statement I made appears in Hansard at page 1269, as follows:
After the house was adjourned early in August I went back to my constituency and kept silent, but I did witness what was going on. For example, in the latter part of July, shortly before I reached home, on a sunny day exactly at noon, at Griffon cove which is right opposite my home, a battle was engaged between a submarine and two corvettes. As the battle was starting Mr. Laurent Giroux, a building contractor, rushed to a telephone and called the Gaspe operator, telling her to pass the word to Gaspe military base, where we were supposed to have some bombers.
Here is what I find in the minister's answer as reported at page 1342 of Hansard, in the last paragraph of the first column:
He referred to an important battle which had taken place near his home, off Griffon cove.
He was referring to me. He continued:
I must tell him that he has not had the privilege of witnessing a battle at all, and that all he heard was gun practice between two corvettes which were going up the river.
The minister misinterpreted my statement, because I had not said I had heard or seen anything myself on that occasion. It is likely on account of that statement of the minister that the Ottawa Journal of March 19 published an ediorial entitled "Mr. Roy didn't see a Battle." The editorial states:
The Budget-Mr. Roy

Standing on his Gaspe cliffs one day last summer, Mr. J. S. Roy, who is Gaspe's M.P., saw two corvettes two miles out at sea racing about like mad and firing their guns, decided he was having a grandstand view of a naval battle. Mr. Roy was disturbed, he could not see any enemy craft, but this surely was a struggle between two of Canada's corvettes and one or more of Mr. Hitler's U-boats, so why on earth were there no aircraft about to help the corvettes.
The article goes on at more length. I wish to say that it is unfair to me because I had never said that I had witnessed that battle myself.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that I have the right to protest against this accusation. I am not afraid to state that my loyalty to my country cannot be questioned when I honestly endeavoured to bring about a better protection of the St. Lawrence water route.
If I took this stand before the house, it was after having tried to get the ministers to understand the perilous situation in which our ships were when travelling on the St. Lawrence. In fact, after the two first sinkings I wrote a private letter to the three ministers of national defence. Two of them answered me that everything was O.K., and the third one that the area of the St. Lawrence could be given maximum protection at minimum effort on account of the closeness of the shore bases. Then, as more sinkings happened, I realized that the state of mind which was existing at our national defence headquarters was one of false security of the most dangerous type.
That is the reason why when a short while later, three more ships were sunk opposite Cap Chat, I made the announcement to the house with the purpose of arousing public opinion in order to bring about a change of mind in government officials. Yet I was bitterly rebuked by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, from whose speech I quote this one sentence as reported at page 2126 of Hansard of the 1942 session:
I am not ready to change the disposition of one ship of the Canadian navy for him or for all the questions he may ask from now till doomsday.
Doomsday should be translated in French by "judgement dernier" or "fin des temps." Thus doors of collaboration were closed to me. But in view of the importance of these events which occurred in the St. Lawrence, and considering further my attitude in this matter, I do not hesitate to leave it to public opinion whether I was disloyal in taking this matter up before the house as I did.
